lessons.ch1s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. Understanding payments in this way helps a business analyst avoid a common mistake, which is to treat every money movement as the same thing.
lessons.ch1s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment versus transfer and apply it to a real banking scenario. A business analyst should be precise even when others are loose.
lessons.ch1s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment instruments and apply it to a real banking scenario. A business analyst must know which instrument fits which use case.
lessons.ch1s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain push versus pull payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst documents push and pull as two different products, not as one payment flow with a flag.
lessons.ch1s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment versus settlement and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the practical lesson is to never confuse a customer credit with final settlement.
lessons.ch1s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain value date, finality and irrevocability and apply it to a real banking scenario. Analysts must capture value date rules explicitly in payment specifications.
lessons.ch1s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain this foundation matters for a BA and apply it to a real banking scenario. A business analyst who understands what a payment really is can ask better questions, write clearer requirements, and spot risks earlier.
lessons.ch2s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain credit transfers, the default business payment. A credit transfer is a payment instruction in which the payer, known as the debtor, instructs the debtor agent to transfer funds to the account of the payee, known as the creditor. For a business analyst, the two questions that matter most about a credit transfer product are how files are processed and when the cut off falls.
lessons.ch2s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain direct debits and pull collections. A direct debit is a pull payment in which the creditor, with the prior authorisation of the debtor, instructs the creditor agent to collect funds from the debtor account through the debtor agent. For a business analyst, direct debits require careful attention to mandates, notifications, and returns.
lessons.ch2s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cards, how a card payment really works. A card payment involves more parties than a simple transfer, and understanding the flow is essential for anyone working in retail payments. A business analyst must distinguish between authorisation, clearing, settlement, and dispute, and must know which system holds the truth at each stage.
lessons.ch2s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cheques, still relevant in some markets. A cheque is a written, signed instruction from an account holder to a bank to pay a named payee a stated amount from the drawer account. For an analyst, cheque work is mostly about the exceptions.
lessons.ch2s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain e-money, wallets and newer instruments. E-money is electronically stored monetary value that represents a claim on the issuer and is accepted as a means of payment by parties other than the issuer. For an analyst, the key is to identify where the value is actually held, who is liable if the wallet provider fails, and how a payment from a wallet settles with the merchant.
lessons.ch2s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain real time versus batch payments. Real time payments settle individually, within seconds, at any time of day, including weekends and holidays. A business analyst must be able to explain when to use each model and what the customer should expect.
lessons.ch2s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain domestic versus cross border, retail versus wholesale. A domestic payment is one where the debtor and creditor accounts are held in the same country and usually in the same currency, and it is processed through a national clearing system. An analyst should state the classification of every payment product in the first paragraph of its specification, domestic or cross border, retail or wholesale.
lessons.ch3s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain debtor and creditor, the two ends of every payment. The debtor is the party who owes the money and who instructs the payment, and the creditor is the party who is owed the money and who receives it. Analysts must therefore treat party data as a core part of the payment, not as a decorative extra.
lessons.ch3s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain debtor agent and creditor agent, the banks that act. The debtor agent is the bank or payment service provider that holds the debtor account and executes the payment instruction on behalf of the debtor. For a business analyst, the agent roles are essential for tracing a payment and for assigning ownership of a failure.
lessons.ch3s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain intermediary banks and correspondent banking. An intermediary bank is a bank that sits between the debtor agent and the creditor agent in a payment chain and helps to move funds when the two agents do not have a direct relationship. As an analyst, you must be able to draw the chain for any payment you work on, name each intermediary, and explain why it is there.
lessons.ch3s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clearing houses and central banks. A clearing house is an institution that receives payment instructions from multiple banks, sorts them, calculates net positions, and prepares them for settlement. Analysts must understand the clearing cycle for each system they work with, including the cut off times, the settlement windows, and the consequences of a bank failing to settle.
lessons.ch3s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to name the scheme for a given payment, read a rulebook extract, map the parties in the four-party card model, trace the money and the fees through authorisation, clearing and settlement, and write a requirement that cites a scheme rule. A scheme is the rulebook that makes payments interoperable. Every payment you build must be traceable to a rule in that book, and a feature that violates scheme rules will be rejected in testing or lead to fines after launch.
lessons.ch3s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain regulators, compliance and oversight. A regulator is a public authority that oversees payment systems, payment institutions, and banks to ensure safety, stability, fairness, and compliance with the law. A business analyst must work closely with compliance teams and must understand the basics of anti money laundering, counter terrorist financing, sanctions screening, and fraud prevention.
lessons.ch3s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain players interact, a single payment story. Consider a simple example. A business analyst who can tell this story, name each player, and explain what each player does is able to diagnose problems quickly, write requirements that reflect reality, and communicate with operations, compliance, and technology teams in a common language.
lessons.ch3s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bank does. A commercial bank is the institution that holds money for people and businesses and moves it when they ask it to. For a business analyst, the practical point is that every payment design must name both layers: which commercial banks hold the customer accounts, and which settlement system and central bank accounts carry the final movement of value.
lessons.ch4s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain initiation, where every payment begins. Every payment travels through seven stages, and this chapter maps the whole journey before it looks at any one stage in detail. A good analyst documents the initiation channel, the mandatory fields, the validation rules, and the error messages for each failure, so that customers and operations teams know exactly what to fix.
lessons.ch4s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain validation, screening and fraud checks. Once a payment instruction is accepted, it enters a stage of validation, screening, and fraud checking that is invisible to most customers but critical to the safety of the system. For a business analyst, this stage requires careful requirements.
lessons.ch4s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authorisation and debit, committing the funds. Authorisation is the step where the debtor confirms that the payment should proceed, and the debtor agent commits the funds. If the debit happens early, the customer sees the money leave quickly, but the bank must manage the funds until settlement.
lessons.ch4s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clearing, routing and message exchange. Clearing is the process by which payment instructions are exchanged between banks, sorted, and prepared for settlement. The message must carry all the information the next bank needs to process the payment, including the debtor and creditor details, the amount, the charges, and the remittance information.
lessons.ch4s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interbank settlement, moving value between banks. Interbank settlement is the movement of value between banks that makes the payment final. Analysts must understand the settlement model for each system they work with, the liquidity requirements, and the contingency arrangements.
lessons.ch4s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain crediting the beneficiary and notification. The final stage of the lifecycle is the credit to the beneficiary and the notification that the payment has arrived. Analysts must document the crediting rules, the return codes, the suspense account handling, and the notification content.
lessons.ch4s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exceptions, returns, recalls and investigations. No payment lifecycle is complete without exception handling, because a significant minority of payments will fail, be delayed, or need investigation. For a business analyst, exception handling is where much of the real work lies.
lessons.ch4s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: how the lifecycle is built inside a bank. A payment lifecycle is implemented as a finite state machine, and every state has a clear owner, a set of allowed transitions, and a set of actions that must complete before the payment can move on. Operations teams use this trail to answer customer queries, investigate delays, and prove compliance during audits.
lessons.ch4s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authentication: proving who you are before the money moves. Authentication is the control that proves who you are before a payment is allowed to move, and it is not the same control as authorisation. For a business analyst, product owner or subject matter expert, the test is to state, for every channel and every payment type, which authentication method applies, what triggers a step-up, what happens when authentication fails, and what evidence is kept.
lessons.ch5s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT MT is. SWIFT MT, where MT stands for Message Type, is the long established messaging standard used by banks around the world to exchange payment instructions and related information. The fixed field structure also makes MT messages relatively easy to parse, to test, and to repair, which operations teams value.
lessons.ch5s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT103, the customer payment. The MT103 is a single customer credit transfer message, and before the CBPR+ migration it was the most widely used cross border payment message in the world. A business analyst must understand the MT103 field structure, the mandatory versus optional fields, and the business meaning of each field, because those details determine whether the payment is processed automatically or falls into a repair queue.
lessons.ch5s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT202, bank to bank cover payments. The MT202 is a general financial institution transfer, and it is used for bank to bank payments where the originator and the beneficiary are both financial institutions. An analyst must be able to explain the cover method, draw the two message flows, and identify where the customer data is visible and where it is not.
lessons.ch5s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT900 and MT910, confirmations of debit and credit. The MT900 is a confirmation of debit, and the MT910 is a confirmation of credit. Analysts should include MT900 and MT910 in their payment flow diagrams and in their reconciliation requirements, because they are the link between the payment instruction and the actual movement of funds.
lessons.ch5s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT940 and mt942, account statements. The MT940 is a customer statement message that provides the end of day statement for an account, usually a nostro or vostro account held with another bank. An analyst who understands MT940 and MT942 will find the camt messages familiar, because the business concepts of opening balance, transactions, and closing balance are the same.
lessons.ch5s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain field structure, how to read an MT message. An MT message is divided into blocks, and the text block contains tagged fields. A business analyst who can read an MT103 can investigate a payment delay, can explain a deduction to a customer, and can write test cases that reflect real payment data.
lessons.ch5s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain to read a real MT103, worked example. This worked example is set before the CBPR+ migration, when an MT103 was still the message for a cross-border customer payment. If the beneficiary receives less than ten thousand dollars, the analyst can use the MT103 to explain why.
lessons.ch5s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: cover method, paris to madrid in USD. This worked example is set before the CBPR+ migration, so the payment travels as an MT103 announcement with an MT202 COV cover. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.
lessons.ch5s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: serial method, the same payment in three mt103s. This worked example is set before the CBPR+ migration, so the payment travels as MT103s. A business analyst who can trace both methods through the same payment, field by field, understands correspondent banking at a level most practitioners never reach.
lessons.ch5s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT message blocks 1 to 5: how to read a raw message. Every SWIFT MT message is built from up to five blocks, each wrapped in curly brackets and numbered 1 to 5. That skill lets an analyst read any MT message without a tool.
lessons.ch5s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: SWIFT connectivity inside a bank. A bank connects to SWIFT through Alliance Access and Alliance Gateway, which together form the bank's SWIFT interface. Operations teams use it to prove that a payment was sent, to investigate a missing payment, and to reconcile SWIFT traffic against the payment engine.
lessons.ch5s12: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt102, many customer transfers in one message. The MT102 is the SWIFT message that carries many customer credit transfers inside a single message. An analyst who meets one should still be able to read it: find the batch total in Sequence C, count the transactions in Sequence B, and reconcile the two before investigating any single payment inside it.
lessons.ch5s13: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt210, notice that funds are coming. The MT210 is an advance notice that funds are on their way, and it moves no money itself. For a business analyst, the MT210 is a control message rather than a payment, and the design questions are about matching rules, suspense handling, and the reconciliation of notices against statements.
lessons.ch5s14: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt191: requesting payment of charges, interest and other expenses. When a bank has incurred charges or interest on behalf of another bank and cannot deduct them from the payment itself, it needs a way to ask for the money. The analyst must check which of the two the business process needs before specifying either.
lessons.ch5s15: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt195, mt196, mt199 and mt299: queries, answers and free format messages. Not every message between banks fits a structured payment format. Sometimes one bank needs to ask another a question, answer one, or send a message that does not fit any other type.
lessons.ch5s16: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt104: direct debits and requests for debit transfer. The MT104 is the SWIFT message that pulls money instead of pushing it. A direct debit is a pull on somebody else account, so the debtor bank must be satisfied that the debtor agreed to the debit before it acts.
lessons.ch5s17: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt200, mt201, mt203 and mt204: financial institution transfers and direct debits. Category 2 of the SWIFT MT standard holds the messages banks use to move money between themselves. Four of them form a family that every payments analyst should be able to tell apart: the MT200, the MT201, the MT203, and the MT204.
lessons.ch5s18: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt670 and mt671: exchanging standing settlement instructions through SWIFT. Every payment needs to know where to settle, and that knowledge is a standing settlement instruction, usually shortened to SSI. For a business analyst, the lesson is about static data discipline.
lessons.ch5s19: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt198: the proprietary message. Not every exchange between banks fits a standard message. A business analyst should treat every proprietary message as a liability to be managed: documented, versioned, and reviewed regularly against the question of whether a standard message now covers the need.
lessons.ch6s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 is. ISO 20022 is an international standard for financial messaging that defines a common language for exchanging payment, securities, trade, and other financial information. For a business analyst, ISO 20022 is important because it changes how payment data is modelled.
lessons.ch6s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 replaced MT. SWIFT MT served the industry well for decades, but it has limitations that became more pressing as payments became faster, more complex, and more regulated. An analyst must be able to explain these benefits to stakeholders who see only the cost of migration, because the business case depends on those benefits being realised in operations, not just on the technical ability to send a new message format.
lessons.ch6s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain XML structure, how an ISO 20022 message is built. An ISO 20022 message is an XML document with a clear, hierarchical structure. A business analyst does not need to be an XML developer, but must be able to read an ISO 20022 message, identify the key elements, and explain what each element means.
lessons.ch6s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain business model behind the messages. Behind every ISO 20022 message is a business model that defines the concepts, the relationships, and the rules that the message expresses. For an analyst, the business model is a tool for writing clear requirements.
lessons.ch6s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message catalogue, PACS, PAIN and CAMT. The ISO 20022 message catalogue is organised by business area, and the three most important areas for payments are pacs, pain, and camt. The catalogue is large, and it continues to grow, but an analyst does not need to memorise every message.
lessons.ch6s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain adoption timeline and CBPR plus. ISO 20022 adoption followed a phased timeline, and the cross-border migration is now complete. For a business analyst, the timeline matters because it explains the state of the systems you work on.
lessons.ch6s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain changes for banks, corporates and operations. For banks, ISO 20022 migration requires changes to payment engines, to screening systems, to reconciliation systems, and to customer channels. Analysts who work with corporates must be able to explain both the benefit and the cost, and must help corporates plan their own migration.
lessons.ch6s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 fundamentals with annotated XML samples. ISO 20022 is a standard for financial messaging that defines messages in XML, and the best way to learn it is to read a real message, line by line, with each element explained. Takeaway: a pacs.008 is a Document with a Group Header, a Payment Information block and a Credit Transfer Transaction Information block, and each element has a purpose, a format and a rule.
lessons.ch6s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT versus mx worked comparison: the same payment as MT103 and as pacs.008, field by field. The same payment can be written as an MT103 and as a pacs.008, and comparing the two field by field is the fastest way to understand why ISO 20022 replaced MT. Takeaway: the same USD 25,000 payment is an MT103 with numbered fields and 140 characters of remittance, and a pacs.008 with named elements, structured addresses and structured remittance.
lessons.ch6s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain business application header, head.001. The Business Application Header, known as head. Takeaway: head.001 is the envelope for an ISO 20022 business message, with From, To, BizMsgIdr, MsgDefIdr, BizSvc and CreDt, and it is read before the business content.
lessons.ch6s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain value versus non-value messages. Payment messages divide into two kinds, and the division shapes how they are processed, controlled, and tested. For a business analyst, the classification drives requirements, testing, and monitoring.
lessons.ch6s12: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain actc: the accepted technical validation status. When a bank receives a payment instruction, the first thing it checks is whether the message itself is valid: is it well formed, properly authenticated, and compliant with the schema and the usage guideline?. For a business analyst, status mapping is precision work.
lessons.ch7s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pacs.008 is and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst must be able to distinguish those three messages, because they have different structures, different mandatory fields, and different business meanings.
lessons.ch7s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain group header, the message envelope and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the Group Header is important because it is the first place to look when a message fails validation.
lessons.ch7s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment information, the batch level details and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst must understand this hierarchy, because it affects how messages are constructed, how they are validated, and how errors are handled.
lessons.ch7s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain credit transfer transaction, the single payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst must be able to read a transaction block, identify each element, and explain its business meaning.
lessons.ch7s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain key fields explained with examples and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst should know which codes are used in the relevant usage guideline, and should ensure that test data covers each code that the product supports.
lessons.ch7s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain line by line walkthrough of a pacs.008 and apply it to a real banking scenario. If the beneficiary receives less than ten thousand dollars, the analyst can point to the Charge Bearer SHAR and explain that charges were shared.
lessons.ch7s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain common errors and validation in pacs.008 and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, validation requirements must be precise.
lessons.ch7s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: processing pacs.008 at scale and apply it to a real banking scenario. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.
lessons.ch8s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain migration was needed. Migration from MT to ISO 20022 was needed because MT could no longer carry the rich, structured data that modern payments require, and because domestic schemes around the world were adopting ISO 20022 independently,. For a business analyst, the end of coexistence changes the work.
lessons.ch8s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain translation rules, how MT becomes mx and back. Translation between MT and MX is governed by mapping rules defined by SWIFT and by the CBPR Plus usage guidelines. For a business analyst, the translation deliverables were concrete.
lessons.ch8s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mapping types, direct, split, derived and needs care. SWIFT defines several mapping types to describe how MT and MX fields relate to each other, and understanding those types helps an analyst assess the risk of a given translation. SWIFT defines several mapping types to describe how MT and MX fields relate to each other, and understanding those types helps an analyst assess the risk of a given translation.
lessons.ch8s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain truncation risk, the silent data loss. Truncation risk is the risk that data is lost when a longer MX field is translated to a shorter MT field, and it is one of the most important risks in the MT to MX migration. An analyst who understands truncation risk can write requirements that minimise it, and can explain to stakeholders why a payment that looks correct in MX may fail after translation to MT.
lessons.ch8s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain banks must do, readiness and testing. Banks that migrate to ISO 20022 must undertake a programme of work that covers technology, operations, compliance, and customer readiness. On the compliance side, sanctions screening, anti money laundering, and fraud rules must be updated for the new data model, and the bank must be able to demonstrate to regulators that its controls work in both formats.
lessons.ch8s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CBPR plus usage guidelines and scheme rules. The CBPR Plus usage guidelines define how ISO 20022 messages must be used for cross-border payments. For a business analyst, the usage guidelines are the primary reference for any ISO 20022 project.
lessons.ch8s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain post-migration checklist for a BA: what to verify now that MT103 and MT202 are gone for cross-border payments. Now that coexistence has ended on 22 November 2025 and MT103 and MT202 are gone for cross-border payments, the BA checklist has changed. Confirm that the operations team can read an ISO 20022 message and investigate a payment without needing to translate it to MT.
lessons.ch8s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt101 to pain.001: the same corporate instruction mapped field by field. The MT101 Request for Transfer and the pain.001 Customer Credit Transfer Initiation carry the same business instruction in two different formats. The analyst must record a business decision, a fallback behaviour, and a manual review path for each needs care field.
lessons.ch8s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hvps+ and CBPR+: the high value rulebook and which rulebook applies. The HVPS+ rulebook is the set of SWIFT ISO 20022 usage guidelines written for high value payment systems and market infrastructures. A bank must therefore validate inbound messages against CBPR+ at the border and against HVPS+ at the settlement system, and it must test the handover explicitly.
lessons.ch8s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cgi-mp, common usage guidelines for corporates and banks. CGI-MP is the agreed common way for corporates and banks to use ISO 20022 messages in practice. For a business analyst, the requirements should cite the CGI-MP guideline and version, the test plan should include cases that break usage rules as well as cases that pass them, and the onboarding checklist should confirm the bank support statement before the first live file.
lessons.ch8s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction manager in depth: the central record of an ISO 20022 payment. When a payment travels through several banks, each bank sees only its own leg, and no single bank holds the complete picture of the transaction from end to end. It is the data backbone of the CBPR+ migration, and the analyst who designs cross border flows must understand what it stores, who can access it, and what problems it solves.
lessons.ch8s12: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain edifact: the older standard that still carries trade and payment data. Long before ISO 20022, and alongside SWIFT, another messaging standard was already moving business data between organisations: UN/EDIFACT, the United Nations rules for Electronic Data Interchange for Administration,. Any analyst working on legacy integrations will meet it.
lessons.ch8s13: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ansi x12 and the 820: payment orders in the north american standard. In North America the dominant electronic data interchange standard is ASC X12, usually shortened to ANSI X12 after the American National Standards Institute that accredits it. The payment transaction set, and the one a payments analyst is most likely to meet, is the 820: the Payment Order and Remittance Advice.
lessons.ch8s14: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message conversion in depth: translating MT to mx without losing meaning. Migration from MT to ISO 20022 needs translation. The analyst job is to make conversion boring: specified, tested, and monitored, so that migration changes the format without changing the money.
lessons.ch9s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain indian payments landscape at a glance. India runs one of the most layered domestic payment systems in the world, and a business analyst who works on Indian payments needs to understand how the layers fit together rather than treating each rail as a separate. India runs one of the most layered domestic payment systems in the world, and a business analyst who works on Indian payments needs to understand how the layers fit together rather than treating each rail as a separate product.
lessons.ch9s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UPI architecture: vpa, psp banks and NPCI. UPI turns a bank account into a simple address. An analyst who confuses the PSP bank with the remitter bank will misassign responsibility when a payment fails.
lessons.ch9s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain IMPS: instant transfers around the clock. IMPS was India's first truly instant account to account transfer system. Because the service never sleeps, banks must keep their IMPS interfaces available at all hours, and operations teams must handle failures at 3 in the morning just as well as at 3 in the afternoon.
lessons.ch9s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NEFT: batch settlement and why it still matters. NEFT is the Reserve Bank of India batch based system for transferring money between bank accounts across India. The analyst must never let the screen promise instant credit for an NEFT payment.
lessons.ch9s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain RTGS: high value settlement with finality. RTGS is the Reserve Bank of India system for high value transfers where each payment is settled individually and immediately in the books of the central bank. To settle a payment, the sending bank must have enough funds in its settlement account at the exact moment of settlement.
lessons.ch9s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NACH: bulk debits, credits and recurring payments. NACH is the NPCI system for bulk and recurring payments, and it is the quiet workhorse behind salaries, EMIs, insurance premiums, utility bills, and mutual fund SIPs. Returns arrive in files that the presenting bank must reconcile record by record.
lessons.ch9s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rails differ: limits, timing and cost. The fastest way to compare the Indian rails is to put them side by side on four questions. Timing is where analysts most often make mistakes, because the words instant and same day mean different things on different rails.
lessons.ch9s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain choosing the right rail: a worked example. Consider a mid sized company in Bengaluru that needs to make four payments on the same morning, ten thousand rupees to a vendor who supplied office stationery, one lakh fifty thousand rupees to a consultant, twenty five. A good analyst would not send all four through the same rail.
lessons.ch9s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain runs indian payments: the RBI, NPCI and the ifsc. Indian payments rest on three distinct parts that a beginner must keep separate, namely the regulator, the operator, and the addressing code. The analyst must state, for each requirement, whether the rule comes from the regulator or the rail is operated by the Reserve Bank, because the RBI acts as both rule setter and operator.
lessons.ch10s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain US payments landscape at a glance. The United States runs its domestic payments on a mix of old and new systems, and the mix can confuse anyone who expects a single national design like the one India built around NPCI. A business analyst working on US payments must learn which operator runs each system, because the operator decides the rules, the hours and the support model.
lessons.ch10s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FEDWIRE: the federal reserve's RTGS system. Fedwire Funds Service is the real time gross settlement system operated by the Federal Reserve. Operating hours and cutoffs are the hard deadlines that operations teams watch closely.
lessons.ch10s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FEDNOW: instant payments around the clock. FedNow Service is the Federal Reserve's instant payment system, launched in July 2023. The analyst must design the funding and alerting rules with treasury, because a bank that runs out of FedNow liquidity on a Sunday night cannot wait until Monday morning.
lessons.ch10s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ACH: the batch network that pays america. The Automated Clearing House, or ACH, is the electronic network that moves most of the routine payments in the United States. The whole cycle takes one to two business days for a standard ACH payment, and the analyst must make this timing clear, because the customer experience can look fast while settlement is still a day away.
lessons.ch10s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CHIPS: private sector netting for large payments. Clearing House Interbank Payments System, or CHIPS, is the private sector system operated by The Clearing House for large value US dollar payments. The analyst must show the cutoff in the product and in the operations manual in Eastern Time, and must design the queue view so operations can see which payments are waiting and what funding is needed to release them.
lessons.ch10s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain US payment flows end to end. Consider a company in Chicago that needs to pay a supplier in New York fifty thousand dollars today, pay its employees on Friday, and send two million dollars to a partner bank as part of a securities settlement. A good analyst would route these three payments through three different systems.
lessons.ch10s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain choosing between FEDWIRE, FEDNOW, ACH and CHIPS. The choice between the four systems comes down to four questions that an analyst should ask for every payment. The choice between the four systems comes down to four questions that an analyst should ask for every payment.
lessons.ch10s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FEDWIRE and CHIPS ISO 20022 migrations: complete. The two largest US dollar payment systems have both completed their ISO 20022 migrations. For a business analyst, the practical impact is that US payment projects now assume ISO 20022.
lessons.ch10s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain lynx, canada's high-value RTGS system. Lynx is the system that settles large and time critical payments in Canadian dollars between financial institutions in Canada. The cost is liquidity: a bank must fund each payment in full, not only a smaller net amount at the end of the day.
lessons.ch10s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nss, the national settlement service. The National Settlement Service settles the money behind private sector clearing arrangements in the United States, using accounts at the Federal Reserve. Timing is what most often confuses analysts, because clearing, customer posting and interbank settlement happen at different moments.
lessons.ch10s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain phixius, the ACH information exchange. Phixius is a payment information network run by Nacha, the organisation that governs the ACH network in the United States. Coverage is therefore the limit an analyst should check first: where no responder covers an account, the bank must fall back on other validation methods, such as a prenote or a small test transaction.
lessons.ch10s12: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain aba routing numbers: how US payments find the right bank. Every electronic payment in the United States needs to identify the receiving bank, and the key for that is the ABA routing number: nine digits that identify a specific financial institution. The two numbers are always used together, and the analyst must treat them as a pair.
lessons.ch11s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA. The Single Euro Payments Area, known as SEPA, is one of the most ambitious payment projects in the world. For a business analyst, SEPA is a lesson in how standardisation creates scale.
lessons.ch11s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain IBAN and the SEPA account identifier. The International Bank Account Number, or IBAN, is the account identifier that makes SEPA possible, and every analyst who works on European payments must understand its structure. The International Bank Account Number, or IBAN, is the account identifier that makes SEPA possible, and every analyst who works on European payments must understand its structure.
lessons.ch11s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA credit transfer: sct. A credit transfer is a push payment. Duplicates and cut off times cause the failures analysts see most.
lessons.ch11s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA direct debit: sdd. A direct debit is a pull payment. In the B2B scheme the debtor bank must verify the mandate before it debits, because the business debtor gives up the refund right in exchange.
lessons.ch11s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sct inst: instant euro payments. An instant payment settles in seconds, not days. The payee bank must reply with a pacs.002 status report, accepted with status ACCP or rejected with status RJCT, and on acceptance it must credit the payee account at once.
lessons.ch11s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain target2 and T2: the eurosystem RTGS. TARGET2, now replaced by its successor system known as T2, is the real time gross settlement system operated by the Eurosystem, which is the European Central Bank together with the national central banks of the euro. A payment submitted after the customer cut off will be processed on the next business day, so the cut off is a hard deadline that corporate treasurers and operations teams plan around.
lessons.ch11s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA works across countries: a worked example. Consider a company headquartered in Amsterdam that employs people in Germany, France and Spain, buys goods from a supplier in Italy, and sells a subscription service to customers in eight countries. The analyst's job is to preserve that invisibility in the product design.
lessons.ch11s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA instruments in depth: sct, sct inst, sdd core, sdd b2b. SEPA, the Single Euro Payments Area, covers euro payments across 34 countries. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.
lessons.ch11s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain messages exchanged in the sct scheme: PAIN, PACS, CAMT. All SEPA messages are based on ISO 20022, using XML syntax. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.
lessons.ch11s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA instant payments regulation: phased obligations from 2025. The SEPA Instant Payments Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2024/886, made instant euro payments mandatory across the euro area in phases, not on a single date. For a business analyst, the IPR creates specific requirements.
lessons.ch11s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain validating an IBAN by hand: the mod-97 check worked. The MOD-97 check is the arithmetic test that catches most typing errors in an IBAN before a payment is sent, and every analyst who works on European payments must be able to work it by hand. The MOD-97 check is the arithmetic test that catches most typing errors in an IBAN before a payment is sent, and every analyst who works on European payments must be able to work it by hand.
lessons.ch11s12: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain eurosic: euro clearing in switzerland. Switzerland has its own currency, the franc, and its own real time gross settlement system, SIC, the Swiss Interbank Clearing system operated by SIX. For a business analyst, the lesson is about how payment systems follow trade and finance rather than borders: where the flows are large enough, a clearing service appears, and the analyst job is to understand its rules, its settlement, and its place in the routing choices available to the bank.
lessons.ch12s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UK payments landscape at a glance. The United Kingdom runs its domestic sterling payments on three main systems that have grown up over different decades and now sit side by side, each serving a distinct purpose. Together they move almost every pound that changes hands inside the UK, and a business analyst who works on UK payments must know all three, because a customer requirement that sounds simple, such as pay this supplier today, can mean three different things depending on the value, the urgency and the cost the customer will accept.
lessons.ch12s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain faster payments: near real time for everyday payments. Faster Payments moves sterling between UK bank accounts in seconds. Netting keeps the liquidity each bank needs far lower than gross settlement would.
lessons.ch12s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CHAPS: high value payments with same day finality. CHAPS is the United Kingdom's real time gross settlement system for high value sterling payments. A payment submitted after the cutoff is processed on the next business day, so conveyancers, corporate treasurers and operations teams plan around it.
lessons.ch12s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain BACS: the three day cycle that pays the nation. BACS is the batch system that has moved most UK regular payments since the late 1960s. Bank holidays extend the timetable, and the analyst must design for the calendar, not just the cycle.
lessons.ch12s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain three systems differ. The fastest way to compare the UK systems is to put them side by side on four questions. Timing is where analysts most often make mistakes in the UK, because the words fast and same day mean different things on different systems.
lessons.ch12s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain confirmation of payee and the fight against fraud. Confirmation of Payee, known as CoP, is a service that checks whether the name entered by the payer matches the name on the account that the sort code and account number identify, and it is now a standard part of the UK. The reimbursement rules for authorised push payment fraud are a second layer of protection that the analyst must understand.
lessons.ch12s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain choosing the right system: a worked example. Consider a small business in Manchester that needs to make four payments on the same morning, fifty pounds to a local supplier for stationery, two thousand pounds to a consultant, one hundred and fifty thousand pounds. A good analyst would not send all four through the same system.
lessons.ch12s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sort codes and account numbers: how UK payments find the right account. Every domestic payment in the United Kingdom needs an address, and that address has two parts: a six digit sort code that identifies the bank branch, and an eight digit account number that identifies the account at that. The analyst who understands this structure can read a UK IBAN at a glance, spot a missing or extra digit, and explain to a customer why an international payment needs the IBAN while a domestic payment needs only the sort code and account number.
lessons.ch13s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain correspondent banking is. Correspondent banking is the arrangement that lets a bank in one country make payments in another country where it has no branch, no licence and no account with the central bank. New solutions, including payment system linkages, central bank digital currency projects and fintech networks, are trying to reduce the dependence on correspondent banking, but for now it remains the backbone of cross border payments, and the analyst must design for the world as it is, not the world as it might become.
lessons.ch13s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro and vostro: two names for the same account. Nostro and vostro are the two words that confuse every new analyst in cross border payments, and the confusion disappears once the perspective is clear. Nostro and vostro are the two words that confuse every new analyst in cross border payments, and the confusion disappears once the perspective is clear.
lessons.ch13s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain banks need correspondent accounts. A bank needs a correspondent account in a currency when it has customers who need to pay or receive in that currency and it cannot settle those payments itself. A bank needs a correspondent account in a currency when it has customers who need to pay or receive in that currency and it cannot settle those payments itself.
lessons.ch13s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain account structures: direct, nested and payable through. Not every bank has a direct correspondent relationship with a bank in every country, and the account structures that fill the gaps are important for an analyst to understand. Not every bank has a direct correspondent relationship with a bank in every country, and the account structures that fill the gaps are important for an analyst to understand.
lessons.ch13s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity in nostro accounts. Liquidity is the most practical problem in correspondent banking, and it is the problem that operations and treasury teams spend most of their time managing. A business analyst who writes requirements for a cross border payment product must include the funding process, the forecasting, and the cut off handling, because a payment product that cannot fund its nostro account cannot send payments at all.
lessons.ch13s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro reconciliation and account statements. Nostro reconciliation is the daily discipline of agreeing the balance of a nostro account between the two banks, and it is one of the most important operational controls in cross border payments. Breaks happen for many reasons, and the analyst must know the common ones.
lessons.ch13s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain compliance, sanctions and de-risking. Correspondent banking is one of the most heavily controlled areas in finance, because a correspondent account can be used to move money for money laundering, for terrorist financing, or for evading sanctions, and the. If a payment mentions a sanctioned person, a sanctioned country or a sanctioned entity, it is stopped, and the correspondent bank must decide whether to reject it, to block it, or to report it.
lessons.ch13s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: nostro account management systems. Nostro accounts are managed in the core banking system as a special class of account, with one record per currency per correspondent bank. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.
lessons.ch13s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cips, china's cross-border payment system. CIPS clears and settles renminbi payments moving across China's borders, giving those payments a dedicated route of their own. For an analyst, the practical questions on a CIPS payment mirror those on any cross border payment, with the participant tier added.
lessons.ch13s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain chats, hong kong's RTGS system. Hong Kong settles interbank payments through CHATS, its real time gross settlement system. For an analyst, CHATS is best understood as four settlement systems sharing one operator and one design, not as a single multicurrency account.
lessons.ch13s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fcdps, china's foreign currency domestic payments. FCDPS and CDFCPS are two names for the same Chinese payment system, and treating them as separate systems is the most common mistake analysts make with this topic. FCDPS and CDFCPS are two names for the same Chinese payment system, and treating them as separate systems is the most common mistake analysts make with this topic.
lessons.ch13s12: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro mirrors. A nostro account is our account with you: a bank holds an account with a correspondent bank in another country, in that country currency, so it can make and receive payments there. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.
lessons.ch13s13: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain lead bank, consortium and syndicate models. Large financings need more than one bank. For a business analyst, syndicated and consortium lending is a payments design problem.
lessons.ch14s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain there and apply it to a real banking scenario. Both methods deliver the money and the information, but they do it in different ways, with different speeds, costs and risks, and the analyst must know which one is being used for any given payment.
lessons.ch14s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain serial flow and apply it to a real banking scenario. If the charges are OUR, which means the sender pays all charges, the sending bank must ensure that each bank in the chain is paid separately, or must send the full amount and settle the charges through a separate arrangement, because the beneficiary must receive the full amount.
lessons.ch14s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cover flow and apply it to a real banking scenario. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.
lessons.ch14s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain serial versus cover: a side by side comparison and apply it to a real banking scenario. Cover can be faster for the beneficiary, because the instruction arrives directly, but it is more complex to operate, because the receiving bank must match the cover funds to the instruction, and a mismatch creates a reconciliation break.
lessons.ch14s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain to use each method and apply it to a real banking scenario. The cover method is the right choice when the sending and receiving banks have no direct relationship, when the funds need to travel through a different route from the instruction, and when the beneficiary bank needs the full information quickly.
lessons.ch14s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain inda, inga, cove and clrg codes and apply it to a real banking scenario. The bank must screen the cover payment using the originator and beneficiary information carried in the COVE message, and it must pass the funds on to the next bank in the cover chain.
lessons.ch14s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain tracing a payment through either method and apply it to a real banking scenario. The analyst asks each bank in turn whether it received the MT103, when it received it, when it passed it on, and what charge it deducted.
lessons.ch14s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain method-specific cancellations: cancelling a direct, serial or cover payment. Cancelling a payment is not one process. The usual practice is to cancel the cover first, so that no funds are in flight, and then cancel the customer payment, but the exact order depends on the state of each leg, and the analyst must design the coordination as a single case with two cancellation requests, not as two independent cases.
lessons.ch15s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain our, sha and ben: who pays the charges. Every cross border payment passes through several banks, and every bank that handles it charges a fee. The analyst must know whether the bank offers a guaranteed OUR or a best efforts OUR, and must explain the difference to the customer.
lessons.ch15s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked examples: what the beneficiary actually receives. Consider a payment of ten thousand US dollars from a company in India to a supplier in Germany, where the sending bank charges twenty five dollars, the intermediary bank charges fifteen dollars, and the receiving bank. A business analyst who prepares a worked example like this for a customer or for a training session makes the abstract codes concrete, and the customer can then make an informed choice instead of discovering the deduction when the supplier complains.
lessons.ch15s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain foreign exchange: rates, spreads and conversion. Most cross border payments involve a foreign exchange conversion, because the sender holds one currency and the beneficiary needs another. A customer who sends ten thousand dollars and receives the equivalent in euros may not realise that the bank's rate was one percent worse than the market rate, which means the customer paid one hundred dollars for the conversion without seeing a separate charge.
lessons.ch15s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT GPI: what it is and how it changed tracking. SWIFT gpi, which stands for Global Payments Innovation, is a service launched by SWIFT in 2017 that transformed cross border payments by making them faster, more transparent and trackable. A customer who sends a payment can now see that it has been received by the intermediary bank, that it has been forwarded, and that it has been credited to the beneficiary, with timestamps at each step.
lessons.ch15s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UETR: the unique tracking reference. The Unique End to end Transaction Reference, known as the UETR, is the identifier that makes gpi tracking possible, and every analyst who works on cross border payments must understand it. The Unique End to end Transaction Reference, known as the UETR, is the identifier that makes gpi tracking possible, and every analyst who works on cross border payments must understand it.
lessons.ch15s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transparency: fees, rates and time in the open. Transparency is the direction in which cross border payments are moving, driven by regulation, by competition from fintech companies, and by customer expectation. In the past, a customer who sent money abroad was told the amount to be sent and the charge of the sending bank, but was not told the exchange rate, the spread, the charges of the intermediary banks, or the time the payment would take.
lessons.ch15s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain complete cross border payment: putting it together. Consider a company in Bengaluru that needs to pay a supplier in Frankfurt ten thousand euros for a shipment of machinery, and the company holds rupees. A business analyst who can walk through this example, explain each step, and answer the questions that arise at each step, has understood cross border payments at a practical level.
lessons.ch15s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT universal confirmation. SWIFT Universal Confirmation is the rule that a bank receiving a cross border payment must confirm what happened to it. For a business analyst, the design work is to make confirmation automatic: generate the confirmation from the posting event, monitor the two business day window daily, queue unconfirmed items for same day follow up, and test all four outcomes, including the hold and the transfer outside SWIFT.
lessons.ch15s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain foreign exchange market: how currencies are bought and sold for payments. Every cross border payment that changes currency passes through the foreign exchange market, and the analyst who designs payments must understand how that market works, because the rate, the value date and the. Every cross border payment that changes currency passes through the foreign exchange market, and the analyst who designs payments must understand how that market works, because the rate, the value date and the settlement of the currency conversion decide when the beneficiary is paid and how much they receive.
lessons.ch16s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross border payments fail. Most cross border payments arrive without a problem, but a small percentage fail, and the failures matter out of proportion to their number because each failure involves a customer who is waiting for money, a supplier. Most cross border payments arrive without a problem, but a small percentage fail, and the failures matter out of proportion to their number because each failure involves a customer who is waiting for money, a supplier who has not been paid, or a salary that has not arrived.
lessons.ch16s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rejects: stopped before the money moves. A reject happens when a payment is stopped before the funds have moved, usually because the receiving bank or an intermediary bank cannot process the instruction as it stands. The analyst must design the reject handling to be fast and clear.
lessons.ch16s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain returns: the money comes back. A return happens when a payment has been sent and the funds have moved, but the receiving bank cannot credit the beneficiary and sends the money back. The analyst must design the return handling to match the return to the original payment by UETR, to calculate the amount actually returned, to identify any deduction, and to notify the customer with the amount and the reason.
lessons.ch16s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain recalls: asking for the money back. A recall, also called a payment recall or a request for recall, happens when the sending bank asks the receiving bank to return a payment that has already been credited to the beneficiary, usually because the payment. The recall is not guaranteed to succeed, and the analyst must make that clear to the customer.
lessons.ch16s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigations and reason codes. An investigation is the process of finding out what happened to a payment that has not arrived, has arrived for the wrong amount, or has arrived with the wrong information, and it is the most common exception task in. The investigation starts with the customer reporting the problem, and the operations team then traces the payment using the UETR, the gpi tracker, the SWIFT messages, and the correspondent account statements.
lessons.ch16s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain timelines, costs and who bears them. Every exception has a timeline, and the timeline is set by the rules of the payment system, the agreements between banks, and the law of the countries involved. The analyst must include the cost allocation in the requirements, must ensure that the charges are applied correctly, and must ensure that the customer is told upfront what an exception will cost.
lessons.ch16s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain handling exceptions well: a practical playbook. The best exception handling starts before the exception happens, with validation at payment capture, with clear customer instructions, and with a payment flow that prevents the most common errors. The system should detect a reject, a return, a recall or an investigation automatically, should match it to the original payment by UETR, and should alert the operations team without waiting for the customer to complain.
lessons.ch17s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clearing really means. Clearing is the process that sits between a payment instruction and its final settlement. For a business analyst, understanding clearing means understanding where in the flow a payment can be stopped, corrected or returned, and what information is needed at each step to keep the process reliable and auditable.
lessons.ch17s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain from gross payments to net positions. Every payment has a gross value, which is the full amount instructed by the payer. By netting first, a bank needs a much smaller balance, and the cost of holding that balance falls.
lessons.ch17s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bilateral netting in practice. Bilateral netting is the simplest form of netting, and it involves just two parties. An analyst turns this into three artefacts.
lessons.ch17s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain multilateral netting and the clearing house. Multilateral netting extends the same idea across many participants at once. A clearing house coordinates, while a central counterparty guarantees, and an analyst should not confuse the two.
lessons.ch17s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example with three banks. Consider three banks, A, B and C, exchanging payments during one clearing cycle. Operations teams monitor this closely, because a sudden change in net position changes the liquidity a bank must have ready at settlement.
lessons.ch17s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clearing houses and central counterparties. A clearing house is more than a calculator. For a business analyst, the distinction matters when designing system requirements.
lessons.ch17s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain netting matters for risk and liquidity. Netting reduces the amount of money that must move at settlement, and that directly reduces both liquidity risk and settlement risk. There is a trade off that analysts must understand.
lessons.ch17s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: clearing house architecture. A clearing house processes millions of instructions every day, often 10 to 50 million in a large domestic system, with peak rates of 5,000 to 10,000 instructions per second. This reduces the liquidity each bank needs by 90 percent or more in a typical cycle.
lessons.ch17s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hybrid payment systems. A hybrid payment system settles some payments the gross way and others the net way inside a single system. An analyst should never assume that a payment in a hybrid system is final merely because it was accepted.
lessons.ch17s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rtfs and rtns settlement models. RTFS and RTNS are two labels for two different answers to the same question, namely when a payment that is processed in real time actually becomes final. For an analyst, the working question about any system is therefore not how fast it looks, but when finality happens, and the answer decides how credit, customer funds and failure handling must all be managed.
lessons.ch17s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bilateral and multilateral limits. Netting and clearing systems let participants exchange payments through the day and settle the net amounts later. This matters because clearing and settlement are where money actually moves between banks. A mistake here is a settlement failure, a liquidity shortfall, or a loss.
lessons.ch18s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement means after clearing. Settlement is the moment when value actually moves and a payment becomes final and irrevocable. A business analyst needs to know the finality point for every system they work on, because it drives reconciliation, customer funds availability, exception handling and the wording of terms and conditions.
lessons.ch18s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain real-time gross settlement. Real time gross settlement, known as RTGS, settles each payment individually and immediately, as soon as it is received by the system. For an analyst, the queue is a feature to specify, not a detail to leave to the vendor.
lessons.ch18s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain deferred net settlement. Deferred net settlement, often called DNS, is the model used by most retail payment systems. An analyst documents three things for a DNS system.
lessons.ch18s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain prefunded settlement models. In a prefunded settlement model, participants deposit funds in advance into a settlement account, and payments are settled only to the extent that prefunded balance allows. A business analyst designing a prefunded system needs to model the prefund sizing problem carefully, because getting it wrong directly affects customer experience, either through rejected payments or through wasted liquidity.
lessons.ch18s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain comparing the three models. RTGS, deferred net settlement and prefunded settlement each solve a different problem, and the choice between them is a trade off between risk, liquidity and speed. Understanding these regulatory drivers helps a business analyst explain why a system is designed the way it is, rather than simply describing its mechanics.
lessons.ch18s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain choosing a model for a payment system. When a new payment system is designed, the settlement model is one of the earliest decisions, because it shapes everything else. A business analyst working on such a project spends much of their time mapping these interfaces and confirming that the new system and the existing settlement system agree on timing, amounts and responsibilities.
lessons.ch18s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement finality and legal certainty. Settlement finality is the legal protection that makes a payment system trustworthy. A business analyst who is asked to add a reverse button for settled payments should refuse with the legal reason, not with a technical excuse, because the business needs to understand that this is a legal boundary, not a missing feature.
lessons.ch19s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity. Liquidity, in the context of payment systems, is the ready availability of funds in a bank's central bank account to settle payments as they fall due. For a business analyst, liquidity management is where payment operations meet treasury.
lessons.ch19s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain intraday liquidity and central bank accounts. Every bank that participates directly in a payment system holds a settlement account at the central bank. Intraday credit is usually collateralised, meaning the bank must pledge securities such as government bonds to secure it, and it is usually free or very cheap, because the central bank wants payments to flow smoothly.
lessons.ch19s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity saving mechanisms and queuing. When a bank does not have enough funds to settle a payment immediately, the payment system does not necessarily reject it. The analyst's job is to specify the rules that govern the queue, because the rules decide who waits and who does not.
lessons.ch19s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gridlock and how systems resolve it. Gridlock is a situation where several banks are each waiting for funds from another bank in the group, and no bank can settle its queued payments because each one is waiting for the next. For a business analyst, gridlock is a reminder that payment systems are networks, and the behaviour of one participant affects all the others.
lessons.ch19s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity pools and shared arrangements. A liquidity pool is an arrangement where a group of banks, often part of the same banking group, combine their liquidity for settlement purposes. An analyst documents a pooling arrangement in the same way as any shared service.
lessons.ch19s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain central bank facilities and collateral. Central banks provide several facilities that help banks manage intraday liquidity. A business analyst does not need to be a monetary policy expert, but should understand how these facilities affect the cost and availability of liquidity on a given day.
lessons.ch19s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain banks manage liquidity day to day. In practice, liquidity management is a daily routine with a clear rhythm. A business analyst involved in building or improving such a dashboard needs to understand which metrics matter and how quickly they must update to be useful.
lessons.ch19s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nsfr and lcr in depth: the basel liquidity ratios. The Basel III framework added two liquidity ratios that every bank must live with: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio, the LCR, and the Net Stable Funding Ratio, the NSFR. For a business analyst, the ratios are a data and reporting project.
lessons.ch19s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bcbs intraday liquidity monitoring tools. A bank can be solvent at the end of the day and still fail during it. For a business analyst, the monitoring tools are an intraday data project.
lessons.ch19s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain available, reserved and blocked: liquidity position states. A liquidity position is not one number. For a business analyst, position states are a reporting and control design.
lessons.ch20s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement risk really is. Settlement risk is the risk that a payment will not settle as expected, either because the sending party fails to deliver the funds or the asset, or because settlement happens at a different time or in a different. The risk has two dimensions that analysts must separate.
lessons.ch20s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain herstatt collapse of 1974. The most famous example of settlement risk is the collapse of Bankhaus Herstatt, a small German bank, on 26 June 1974. An analyst uses Herstatt as a test, not just a story.
lessons.ch20s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain principal risk, replacement cost and liquidity risk. Settlement risk is usually broken down into three types, and it helps to keep them distinct. This matters because clearing and settlement are where money actually moves between banks. A mistake here is a settlement failure, a liquidity shortfall, or a loss.
lessons.ch20s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain RTGS reduces settlement risk. Real time gross settlement reduces settlement risk by settling each payment immediately and individually in central bank money. Until eleven fifteen in the morning the receiving bank must not release anything against it, because a queued payment is not a settled payment, and treating it as settled is exactly the mistake RTGS is designed to prevent.
lessons.ch20s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment versus payment. Payment versus payment, usually shortened to PVP, is the principle that the two legs of a foreign exchange transaction should settle simultaneously, so that one cannot settle without the other. A business analyst working on foreign exchange systems needs to know for each currency pair and each settlement channel whether PVP applies, because that determines the risk profile of the trade and the controls that must surround it.
lessons.ch20s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CLS and foreign exchange settlement. CLS, originally known as Continuous Linked Settlement, is a global system that provides payment versus payment settlement for foreign exchange trades in eighteen major currencies. Any business analyst working on cross border payments should understand how CLS fits into the overall flow.
lessons.ch20s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain managing residual risk in practice. No system eliminates settlement risk entirely, so banks and payment system operators manage the residual risk with a combination of limits, collateral, monitoring and contingency plans. An analyst writes the default procedure as a runbook, not as a paragraph in a policy document.
lessons.ch20s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clsnow, same-day fx settlement. CLSNow is the service that brings payment versus payment protection to foreign exchange trades that settle on the same day they are agreed. Eligibility can change over time as the service develops, so an analyst should confirm the current list in the CLS rulebook or with the settlement member before assuming a pair is covered.
lessons.ch20s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CLS in detail: timetable and member structure. Foreign exchange settlement carries a famous risk: Herstatt risk, named after the bank whose failure in 1974 left counterparties who had paid one currency leg without receiving the other. For a business analyst, CLS teaches the settlement design pattern that recurs everywhere: link the legs, net the funding, schedule the window, and tier the membership so that the obligations sit with those who can meet them.
lessons.ch21s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain four parties and the card transaction. The four party model is the foundation of every card payment. The cardholder is the customer who owns the card and makes the purchase.
lessons.ch21s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authorization in real time. Authorisation is the real time check that happens while the customer is still at the till or on the checkout page. Step four is the hold, and the analyst must understand how long it lasts.
lessons.ch21s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain happens after the customer leaves. Once the customer has left, the merchant's work is not finished. For a business analyst, the authorisation to capture gap is a source of many edge cases.
lessons.ch21s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain batching and clearing files. Batching is how the acquirer collects captured transactions and prepares them for clearing. A business analyst working on a clearing interface needs to understand the file layout, the field definitions, the validation rules and the error handling procedures.
lessons.ch21s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interchange fees and how money moves. Interchange is the fee that the acquirer pays to the issuer on every card transaction, and it is the largest component of the cost a merchant pays to accept cards. For business analysts, interchange matters because it drives pricing, product design and negotiations.
lessons.ch21s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement between issuer, acquirer and scheme. Settlement is the movement of money that follows clearing, and it is the stage where promises become payments. A transaction that was authorised but never cleared does not appear in settlement at all, which is why clearing discipline, including timely presentment, is a control the analyst must watch.
