lessons.ch21s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain things go wrong. Card transactions can fail at every stage, and each failure has a different cause and a different remedy. The merchant is not funded on time, and the acquirer's operations team works through the night to fix the three records and resubmit.
lessons.ch21s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: card authorization at scale. Card authorization systems process thousands of transactions per second, with large issuers handling 5,000 to 15,000 authorizations per second at peak, such as during holiday shopping or major sales events. The model is updated regularly with new fraud patterns, and its decisions are logged with the score and the top contributing features, so analysts can review why a genuine transaction was blocked and tune the rules.
lessons.ch22s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain card payments need extra protection. Card payments face a basic problem. Every extra step at checkout, every password to remember and every code to type, increases the chance that a genuine customer will abandon their purchase.
lessons.ch22s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain 3D secure 2 works. Three D Secure, often called 3DS, is a protocol that adds an authentication step to online card payments. An analyst specifies 3DS as a data contract, not just a feature.
lessons.ch22s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain frictionless flow versus challenge flow. The frictionless flow and the challenge flow are the two outcomes of EMV 3D Secure version 2, and the choice between them decides the customer experience of every online card payment. Both flows give the same protection and the same liability shift, but they feel very different at checkout, so the analyst must understand what drives the issuer to choose one or the other.
lessons.ch22s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain tokenization and network tokens. Tokenization replaces a sensitive value with a surrogate value that has no meaning on its own. For the analyst, this is a measurable benefit to track: approval rate and fraud rate, tokenized against non tokenized, for the same merchant.
lessons.ch22s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain device tokens and mobile wallets. Device tokens are the form of tokenization that powers mobile wallets such as Apple Pay and Google Pay. The analyst should confirm that refunds, chargebacks and reporting all carry the token through, end to end.
lessons.ch22s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain chargeback lifecycle. A chargeback is the process by which a cardholder disputes a transaction and the funds are returned to them through the card system, rather than directly by the merchant. A business analyst working on dispute processes needs to understand the full lifecycle and the deadlines, because missing a deadline can mean losing a dispute that could have been won.
lessons.ch22s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reason codes and dispute handling. Every chargeback carries a reason code, and the code is the starting point for the whole dispute. The analyst must map each code to its evidence and its workflow.
lessons.ch23s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sanctions exist. Sanctions are restrictions that governments and international bodies place on specific countries, organisations and individuals to achieve a foreign policy or security goal without using military force. For a business analyst, the practical point is that sanctions are not a policy document, they are a live data problem inside the payment flow.
lessons.ch23s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain main sanctions lists. The OFAC Specially Designated Nationals list, usually called the SDN list, is the most widely screened list in the world. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.
lessons.ch23s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain screening works in a payment flow. Screening happens at defined points in the payment lifecycle, and the timing matters as much as the matching itself. A possible match creates an alert in a work queue for a sanctions analyst to review, and the payment waits until the analyst clears it or escalates it.
lessons.ch23s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain name matching and fuzzy logic. Exact name matching would be useless for sanctions screening, because real payment data is messy. A score above a threshold creates an alert, and the threshold is a tuning decision that balances catching real matches against flooding analysts with noise.
lessons.ch23s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain false positives and alert triage. A false positive is an alert where the payment party shares a name with a listed person but is not that person. Each one still has to be reviewed by a trained analyst, because the bank cannot simply assume that a match is harmless.
lessons.ch23s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain true hits and what happens next. A true hit means the payment genuinely involves a sanctioned party, and the response depends on the sanctions programme. For a BA, this is a requirements point: the workflow must distinguish a blocking programme, where funds are frozen in a blocked account, from a rejection programme, where funds are returned to the sender, and it must record every step for the audit trail.
lessons.ch23s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fines, enforcement and lessons. Sanctions failures have produced some of the largest fines in banking history. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.
lessons.ch23s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT sanctions screening service. Every payment a bank sends or receives must be checked against sanctions lists: the lists of persons, entities, and countries that the law forbids doing business with. When a sanctions list changes, the bank needs to know what the change will do to its alert volumes before the change goes live.
lessons.ch24s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain money laundering really looks like. Money laundering is the process of making money from crime look like it came from a legitimate source, so that it can be spent or invested without attracting attention. For a business analyst, the key point is that anti money laundering controls are embedded in ordinary payment and account processes, not bolted on as a separate system.
lessons.ch24s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain KYC and customer due diligence. Know Your Customer, or KYC, is the process of identifying and verifying a customer before the bank does business with them. The bank must be satisfied that it knows who it is dealing with, and that the customer's expected activity makes sense for who they are.
lessons.ch24s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction monitoring. Transaction monitoring is the automated surveillance of customer activity after onboarding, looking for behaviour that does not fit the customer's profile or that matches known laundering patterns. A sudden change, such as a dormant account becoming active, or a customer whose usual pattern is domestic payments suddenly sending money to three new countries, is more suspicious than the absolute value alone.
lessons.ch24s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain suspicious activity reports. A Suspicious Activity Report, known as a SAR in the United States and a Suspicious Transaction Report in many other countries, is the formal report a bank files with its national Financial Intelligence Unit when it. For a BA, the requirements here cover the SAR workflow itself.
lessons.ch24s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain common fraud patterns in payments. Payment fraud takes many forms, but a few patterns account for most losses. For a BA, fraud requirements cover the full lifecycle.
lessons.ch24s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain machine learning in fraud detection. Traditional fraud detection relied on fixed rules, such as flagging any transaction above a set amount, but criminals learn the rules and stay just below them. Explainability matters too, because when a customer's payment is blocked, the bank must be able to explain why, and a regulator may ask how a model reached its decision.
lessons.ch24s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain building a fraud prevention culture. Technology alone will not stop fraud, because criminals adapt faster than systems do. Front line staff are often the first to spot something wrong, such as a customer who seems confused or pressured while making a large transfer, or a business customer whose invoice details have changed unexpectedly.
lessons.ch24s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain APP fraud and the UK psr reimbursement rules. Authorised push payment fraud, known as APP fraud, happens when a customer is tricked into sending money to a criminal. For a business analyst, the reimbursement rules create a full set of requirements.
lessons.ch25s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment hub. A payment hub is a central platform that processes many different payment types through one shared set of services, instead of each product having its own separate system. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch25s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain channels and the gateway. Channels are the places where a payment starts. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch25s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain validation, enrichment and the processing engine. Validation is the set of checks that confirm a payment is complete, correct and allowed before any money moves. For example, take a payment from a corporate customer who sends EUR 50,000 to a supplier but leaves the beneficiary bank identifier blank.
lessons.ch25s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud, sanctions and compliance services. Fraud and sanctions services sit in the middle of the hub pipeline, and a payment cannot proceed until they have cleared it. The audit trail is critical, because a regulator may ask why a particular payment was released, and the bank must be able to show the fraud score, the sanctions result, the analyst's decision and the timestamp for each step.
lessons.ch25s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain routing, clearing and settlement. Routing is the decision about how a payment leaves the bank and reaches the beneficiary. The hub's settlement handling also covers liquidity management, because the bank needs enough funds in the right accounts to settle its payments.
lessons.ch25s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ledger, reconciliation and reporting. The ledger is the accounting heart of the hub, recording every movement of money as a double entry. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch25s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain design patterns and what good looks like. Several design patterns appear in almost every well built payment hub. For a BA, the practical takeaway is that hub requirements are never just about the happy path.
lessons.ch25s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: building a payment hub. A payment hub is built around five core components that work in sequence. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch26s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain from files and SWIFT to real time APIs. For most of banking history, payments moved through files and messages that were exchanged in batches. For a business analyst, the API shift changes the nature of the work.
lessons.ch26s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain REST APIs for payments. Most modern payment APIs use REST, which is an architectural style built on standard HTTP methods and on resources that have clear identifiers. This matters because APIs and integrations are how systems talk to each other. A badly specified API is a failed payment, a duplicate, or a security hole.
lessons.ch26s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 APIs. ISO 20022 began as a messaging standard for payment instructions, with well known messages such as pain.001 for customer credit transfers and pacs.008 for interbank transfers. This matters because APIs and integrations are how systems talk to each other. A badly specified API is a failed payment, a duplicate, or a security hole.
lessons.ch26s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain PSD2 and open banking. The European Union's second Payment Services Directive, known as PSD2, changed the relationship between banks and their customers by giving customers the right to share their account data with third parties. For a BA, open banking work means understanding the regulatory requirements, the consent model, the API specifications, and the liability rules, because when a third party initiates a payment that goes wrong, the question of who is responsible must have a clear answer.
lessons.ch26s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain customer authentication: mfa, SCA and step-up. Customer authentication is the step where the customer proves who they are to the bank before an API is allowed to act for them, and it is separate from what the API is then allowed to do. For a business analyst, product owner or subject matter expert, the test is to state, for every channel and every payment type, which authentication method applies, what triggers a step-up, what happens when authentication fails, and what evidence is kept.
lessons.ch26s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain webhooks and event driven payments. Polling is the simplest way for a client to learn what happened to a payment. The bank must sign each webhook payload so the client can verify it really came from the bank, and the client must return a success response quickly, so the bank knows the notification was received.
lessons.ch26s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment initiation and the developer experience. Payment initiation is the API use case that changes the checkout experience most visibly. For a BA, the commercial requirements, pricing, service levels, and support commitments, are as important as the technical ones, because they shape what the API can promise to its users.
lessons.ch26s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: payment APIs at scale. The API gateway is the front door for all payment APIs, and it handles routing, security, and traffic management before any request reaches a backend service. This matters because APIs and integrations are how systems talk to each other. A badly specified API is a failed payment, a duplicate, or a security hole.
lessons.ch26s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system authentication: OAuth2 grants, scopes, tokens and certificates. System authentication is the control where one system proves its identity to another system, with no person involved. For a business analyst, product owner or subject matter expert, the test is to state, for every system to system call, which grant type applies, which scopes the token carries, how long the token lives, how it is refreshed, whether mTLS is required, and how certificates are rotated.
lessons.ch27s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain central bank digital currencies. A central bank digital currency, or CBDC, is digital money issued directly by a central bank, as a liability of the central bank itself, in the same way that physical cash is. For a BA, the practical point is that CBDCs are not a distant theory, they are a real product area, and the requirements skills used for any payment product, user journeys, limits, privacy, reconciliation and reporting, apply directly to them.
lessons.ch27s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain stablecoins and crypto payments. A stablecoin is a crypto asset designed to hold a stable value, usually by being pegged to a fiat currency such as the US dollar. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.
lessons.ch27s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in fraud detection and operations. Artificial intelligence is already embedded in payment fraud detection, and its role is growing. Generative AI is being used to help analysts, by summarising a case, drafting a suspicious activity report narrative, or searching through transaction histories in response to a question in plain language.
lessons.ch27s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross border innovation: mbridge and project nexus. Cross border payments have been slow and expensive for decades, because they rely on correspondent banking, where a payment passes through several banks, each taking a fee and adding a delay, and where the sender often. For a BA, the lesson from both projects is that cross border innovation is not about one technology winning, it is about solving the same problems in different ways.
lessons.ch27s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain tokenisation and programmable money. Tokenisation is the process of representing a real world asset, such as a bank deposit, a bond, or a property, as a digital token on a ledger, so that it can be transferred and settled more efficiently. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.
lessons.ch27s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain is real and what. Payments attract more hype than most industries, because money is universal and every new technology claims it will transform how money moves. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.
lessons.ch27s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain this means for a payments BA. The emerging topics in this chapter all point in the same direction for a business analyst. The emerging topics in this chapter all point in the same direction for a business analyst.
lessons.ch27s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain stablecoin regulation in 2026: MICA and beyond. Stablecoin regulation has moved from discussion to law. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.
lessons.ch27s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai across payments: reconciliation, fraud, customer service and operational decisions. Artificial intelligence is already working in payments, and it works in four places: reconciliation, fraud, customer service, and operational decisions. It predicts the liquidity a bank must hold for instant payments by learning the pattern of outbound flows through the day.
lessons.ch27s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ripple overview: ripplenet, xrp and on-demand liquidity. Ripple is a company whose products aim at the same problem as SWIFT gpi and the instant payment links: making cross border payments faster and cheaper. For a business analyst, the lesson is to evaluate the approach on its mechanics: how does the payment move, where does the liquidity come from, who bears the risk, and what does the regulator say.
lessons.ch27s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain agentic payment protocols, part 1: mcp, a2a and the agent stack. An AI agent is software that perceives, decides, and acts on behalf of a user, carrying out multi-step tasks without a human driving each step. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.
lessons.ch27s12: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain agentic payment protocols, part 2: ap2, tap, agent pay, acp, ucp and x402. Six protocols, from six different parts of the industry, aim at the same problem: how does an AI agent pay safely?. For a business analyst, the evaluation questions are the same for all six: what is the trust model, which rails carry the money, who governs the protocol, and what happens when something goes wrong?
lessons.ch28s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain requirements gathering for payments projects. Requirements gathering is the first and most important phase of any payments project, because a requirement missed at this stage becomes a defect, a delay or a failed audit later. A business analyst starts by identifying every stakeholder group that touches the payment flow.
lessons.ch28s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain business process modelling: as-is and to-be flows. Business process modelling turns a spoken description of how payments work into a diagram that everyone can read, challenge and agree on. The analyst always models the As-Is process first, which is how the payment flows today, including every manual step, every workaround and every delay.
lessons.ch28s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain business rules and processing conditions. Business rules are the conditions that decide how a payment is processed, and in payments they are numerous, precise and often invisible until one of them is broken. The analyst's job is to find every rule, write it down in plain language, and make sure the system enforces it exactly.
lessons.ch28s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain writing jira user stories for payments. A user story is a short description of a feature written from the perspective of the person who needs it, and it is the unit of work that agile payments teams build, test and release. A story without a testable acceptance criterion cannot be built or tested, so the analyst who writes the criterion decides whether the developer builds the right mapping and whether the tester can prove it.
lessons.ch28s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain API analysis and interface specifications. An application programming interface, or API, is how one system asks another system to do something, and in payments the most common API is the payment initiation API, which lets a channel such as internet banking ask. The interface specification is the contract between the two systems, and the business analyst reads it to confirm that it covers every field, every validation and every error the business needs.
lessons.ch28s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain BRD and FSD documents for payments. The Business Requirements Document, or BRD, records what the business needs and why, without describing how the system will be built. Consider a project to integrate UPI collect requests into a bank's corporate banking portal, so that a merchant can raise a collect request of 2,500 rupees against a customer who then approves it in their UPI app.
lessons.ch28s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain workshop facilitation: running a payments discovery workshop. A discovery workshop brings all the stakeholders into one room, or one video call, for a focused session to agree on requirements, and it is the fastest way to resolve the questions that stall a payments project. The analyst plans the workshop like any other deliverable.
lessons.ch28s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain BA artefacts that carry a payment design: mapping sheets, sequence diagrams and flow diagrams. A payment design lives or dies by its artefacts. The business analyst does not just describe what should happen; the analyst produces documents that developers can build from, testers can test from, and operations teams can support.
lessons.ch29s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone brief: BA on a SWIFT MT to ISO 20022 migration. You are the business analyst assigned to a migration project at a mid-sized bank in Mumbai that sends around 12,000 outward cross-border payments a day, and your job is to move those payments from SWIFT MT format to ISO. You are the business analyst assigned to a migration project at a mid-sized bank in Mumbai that sends around 12,000 outward cross-border payments a day, and your job is to move those payments from SWIFT MT format to ISO 20022.
lessons.ch29s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT MT103 to ISO 20022 pacs.008 message mapping. A mapping document is a table that lists every field in the source message, the matching field in the target message, and the rule that converts one into the other, and it is the single most important deliverable of the migration. A mapping document is the single most important deliverable of the migration: if a field maps to the wrong element, the payment fails schema validation or settles the wrong amount, so the analyst who writes it decides whether the migration works.
lessons.ch29s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain API business data, rules and validations. The payment initiation API is the front door to the new ISO 20022 world, and it accepts payment instructions from channels such as internet banking, mobile banking and the corporate file upload service. This matters because this is the work a payments BA, PO or SME actually produces: requirements, mappings, stories, test cases and traceability. It is the job, not the theory.
lessons.ch29s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain user stories and acceptance criteria for the migration. The first user story covers the core conversion. As a reconciliation analyst, I want a daily report showing every MT103 received and its converted pacs.008, so that I can prove no payment was lost or altered during migration.
lessons.ch29s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UAT scenarios and end-to-end test cases. A test case is a structured instruction that tells the tester exactly what to do and what result to expect, and it has a fixed format. This matters because this is the work a payments BA, PO or SME actually produces: requirements, mappings, stories, test cases and traceability. It is the job, not the theory.
lessons.ch29s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hands-on BA deliverables checklist. The Business Requirements Document is the first deliverable on the checklist, and it is complete only when it states the business objectives, the scope with explicit exclusions, the prioritised requirements, the. The analyst keeps the signed version in the project repository and versions every change after sign-off.
lessons.ch29s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone exercise: trace a card payment end to end. The exercise starts at checkout, where a customer in Bengaluru buys a laptop for 85,000 rupees on an e-commerce website and pays with a Visa debit card. This matters because this is the work a payments BA, PO or SME actually produces: requirements, mappings, stories, test cases and traceability. It is the job, not the theory.
lessons.ch29s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone: an australian bank joins the npp. The capstone brief places you as the business analyst for a mid-sized Australian bank in Brisbane that has decided to join the NPP. The capstone brief places you as the business analyst for a mid-sized Australian bank in Brisbane that has decided to join the NPP.
lessons.ch29s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone: a US bank joins the rtp network. The capstone brief places you as the business analyst for a regional bank in Ohio joining the RTP network to offer real-time payments. The capstone brief places you as the business analyst for a regional bank in Ohio joining the RTP network to offer real-time payments.
lessons.ch30s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment gateway does. A payment gateway is the technology layer that sits between a merchant website or mobile application and the banking system. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch30s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gateway services. The payment page is the customer facing part of a gateway, and it must be fast, secure and easy to use. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch30s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gateway APIs. A gateway REST API is a set of secure web endpoints that a merchant system calls to create payments, check status and issue refunds. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch30s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain routing and retries. Smart routing is the decision a gateway makes, in milliseconds, about which acquirer should handle a given transaction. A gateway that offers only one acquirer cannot fail over, so multi acquirer support is a key question for a business analyst to ask during vendor evaluation.
lessons.ch30s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment aggregators vs gateways. A payment gateway is primarily a technology service. A business analyst must check the authorization status of any aggregator on the Reserve Bank website before recommending it, because an unauthorized aggregator puts the merchant at risk of frozen settlements and regulatory action.
lessons.ch30s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bas write gateway integration requirements. The work starts with a clear business objective and scope, written before any technical detail. The analyst also documents edge cases, error handling and the go live checklist, which are easy to forget.
lessons.ch30s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gateway fees and commercial models. The merchant discount rate, usually shortened to MDR, is the main fee a merchant pays on each card transaction, expressed as a percentage of the transaction value. The analyst must model the total cost, not just the headline percentage.
lessons.ch31s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain card network roles. A card network is the rails that connect the issuing bank, which gives the card to the customer, with the acquiring bank, which serves the merchant. The cardholder is the customer who holds the card and makes the purchase.
lessons.ch31s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain visa message flow. A Visa authorization starts when the merchant sends a request through the acquirer to VisaNet, which is Visa global processing network. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.
lessons.ch31s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mastercard message flow. A Mastercard authorization also starts with an ISO 8583 message from the merchant, through the acquirer, to the Mastercard network. When a business analyst writes an integration requirement for a Mastercard connection, the MIP is the component that must be installed, certified and tested, and certification includes test cases for approvals, declines, reversals, refunds and stand in processing.
lessons.ch31s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authorization, capture, clearing, settlement. Authorization is the real time check that the card is valid and the funds are available. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.
lessons.ch31s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interchange and scheme fees. Interchange is the fee that the acquirer pays to the issuer on every card transaction, and it is the largest component of the merchant discount rate. A business analyst who evaluates a gateway or acquirer must ask for the full fee schedule, including the rate for each card type, the cross border surcharge, the chargeback fee and the monthly minimum, and must model the cost using the merchant real transaction mix.
lessons.ch31s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NFC and contactless. Near field communication, known as NFC, is a short range wireless technology that lets a card or phone communicate with a payment terminal when held within about four centimetres. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.
lessons.ch31s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain chargebacks. A chargeback starts when a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank, instead of asking the merchant for a refund. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.
lessons.ch31s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 8583 in depth: message types, data elements and the clearing message. ISO 8583 is the message standard for card transactions, and it is the language that the terminal, the acquirer, the scheme and the issuer use to talk to each other. For a business analyst, ISO 8583 is a message specification subject.
lessons.ch32s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain digital wallet architecture: where the money actually sits. A digital wallet is a prepaid stored value account held by a licensed issuer, and the balance you see on your phone is a claim on the issuer rather than money sitting in your own bank account. A business analyst must document this clearly, because confusing a wallet balance with a bank deposit leads to wrong requirements for interest, deposit insurance and account closure.
lessons.ch32s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain wallet transactions: load, pay, send and withdraw. Loading money into a wallet is a pull from a funding source, and the most common sources are UPI, a debit card, net banking or a bank transfer. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.
lessons.ch32s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain wallet KYC: minimum KYC, full KYC and RBI PPI rules. Minimum KYC is the lighter tier, designed to let a customer start using a wallet quickly with only a mobile number verified through an OTP and basic details such as name and date of birth. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.
lessons.ch32s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain wallet security: device binding, pin, biometrics and tokenization. Device binding ties a wallet to a specific phone, so that the wallet cannot simply be opened on a different device with a stolen password. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.
lessons.ch32s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain POS systems overview: terminals, taps and swipes. A POS terminal is a certified payment device that captures card data, encrypts it immediately, and sends an authorisation request to the acquiring bank through the card network. From a business analyst perspective, a POS project is not just about the device, it is about the whole merchant journey, onboarding, terminal deployment, transaction processing, settlement, dispute handling and support.
lessons.ch32s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment acceptance at POS: authorization, settlement and reconciliation. Authorisation is the real time check that happens while the customer waits at the counter, and it usually takes two to three seconds. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.
lessons.ch32s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain QR codes and soundbox: payments for small merchants. A QR payment starts with a code that contains the merchant payment address, usually a UPI ID or a merchant identifier, and sometimes the amount and a transaction reference as well. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.
lessons.ch33s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NACH mandate processing in depth: from creation to activation. NACH is the centralised bulk payment system run by NPCI that allows banks and institutions to collect recurring payments from customers through mandates, and to make bulk credit payments such as salaries and dividends. The BA must specify the scanning quality, the image format, the rejection reason codes, and the customer communication for each rejection, because a customer whose EMI mandate is rejected may not know until the first EMI bounces.
lessons.ch33s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NACH debit and credit: presentation, settlement and returns. A NACH debit presentation starts when the user institution prepares a file of all the debits due on a given date and submits it to NPCI, usually one working day before the debit date. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.
lessons.ch33s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bbps: how bharat bill payment works. BBPS is an integrated bill payment system that connects billers, such as electricity distribution companies, telecom operators, gas companies and insurers, to the customers who pay them, through a network of agent. Reconciliation is critical because a customer who has paid must never be marked as a defaulter by the biller.
lessons.ch33s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UPI mandate and autopay: requirements from a BA perspective. A UPI mandate is a standing instruction registered on the UPI platform that authorises a merchant to collect payments from a customer bank account through UPI, up to a defined maximum amount and within a defined period. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.
lessons.ch33s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UPI architecture in depth: vpa, psp apps and the NPCI switch. The Virtual Payment Address, or VPA, is the identifier that makes UPI easy to use, because it replaces the bank account number and IFSC with a simple handle such as learner@okhdfcbank. That is why the bank needs a robust reversal and reconciliation process.
lessons.ch33s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fema compliance for payments it projects. FEMA is the Indian law that regulates foreign exchange transactions, and its core principle is that foreign exchange can only be dealt with through authorised persons, such as banks licensed as authorised dealers, and. A customer who has already remitted 240,000 dollars cannot remit a further 20,000 dollars in the same financial year.
lessons.ch33s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross-border payments from india: SWIFT, nostro, vostro and a worked example. SWIFT messaging is the network that carries the payment instructions between banks, and it is important to understand that SWIFT does not move money, it moves messages about money. A BA must document the charge options offered to the customer, the fee schedule for each option, and the disclosure that the customer sees before confirming the payment, because a customer who expected to receive 10,000 dollars and received 9,950 dollars will raise a complaint if the charges were not explained.
lessons.ch33s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain aeps: aadhaar enabled payment system. AEPS, the Aadhaar Enabled Payment System, is India interoperable banking service that lets a customer perform basic banking transactions at a micro ATM using only their Aadhaar number and their fingerprint, without a. For a business analyst, AEPS is a financial inclusion and operations subject.
lessons.ch33s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain dmt: domestic money transfer. DMT, Domestic Money Transfer, is India service that lets a person send money to any bank account in India using only the recipient mobile number or account number, without needing the recipient bank details or a bank. For a business analyst, DMT is an agent network and compliance subject.
lessons.ch33s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sfms: the structured financial messaging system. India domestic interbank payments run on a messaging system most people outside Indian banking have never heard of: SFMS, the Structured Financial Messaging System. For a business analyst working on Indian payments, SFMS is foundational knowledge.
lessons.ch33s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sdmc, mdmc and umrn: bulk file accounting and the NACH mandate reference. Three identifiers that look like alphabet soup carry real operational meaning in Indian bulk payments and mandates: SDMC, MDMC, and UMRN. For a business analyst, the lesson is that identifiers are infrastructure: the UMRN, like the accounting types, is a small piece of data that the whole operation depends on.
lessons.ch33s12: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ccil: the clearing corporation of india. A central counterparty, a CCP, stands between buyers and sellers in financial markets, guaranteeing settlement even if one side defaults. For a business analyst, CCIL teaches the CCP pattern that applies well beyond India.
lessons.ch34s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain recurring payments explained. A recurring payment is a payment that a merchant initiates on a schedule the customer agreed to in advance, without the customer being present for each charge. From a business analyst perspective, recurring payments are a rich area because they touch almost every system a merchant owns.
lessons.ch34s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain 3D secure requestor initiated (3ri) transactions. 3RI is a message type defined in the EMV 3D Secure version 2 specification, and it allows a merchant to request authentication for a transaction that the merchant initiates rather than the cardholder. For a business analyst, the important details of 3RI are the data elements and the error handling.
lessons.ch34s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain subscribe n save: the mycommerce project scenario. The myCommerce project describes an e-commerce merchant that sells everyday products such as groceries, household goods, and personal care items. The project scenario is used in business analyst training because it forces the analyst to think about the full lifecycle of a subscription, not just the checkout page, and that lifecycle is where the real complexity lives.
lessons.ch34s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain writing a use-case document for system-triggered payments. A use-case document starts with the basic identification fields, and these matter more than people think. A business analyst writes these as a numbered list so that testers can verify each one, and so that developers can code the checks in the right order.
lessons.ch34s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain recurring payment failure handling. The most common cause of recurring payment failure is an expired card. Dunning is the process of communicating with a customer whose payment has failed, and it is a mix of messaging, timing, and tone.
lessons.ch34s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain card-on-file and tokenization for recurring. A card-on-file transaction is any transaction that uses payment credentials a merchant stored from an earlier transaction. From a business analyst perspective, card-on-file design means documenting several connected requirements.
lessons.ch34s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain recurring payments compliance. The Reserve Bank of India introduced its e-mandate framework for recurring card payments in 2019 and tightened it in 2021, and it changed the Indian subscription market completely. The pre-debit notification is the most important customer protection in the RBI framework, and it is a requirement that business analysts must design carefully.
lessons.ch34s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ebpp and eipp: electronic bill and invoice presentment and payment. A bill or an invoice is a request for payment, and presenting it electronically, with the payment attached, removes the friction of paper, post, and manual entry. For a business analyst, EBPP and EIPP design is three disciplines at once.
lessons.ch35s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain end-to-end payment platform design. Designing a payment platform from scratch starts with the business requirements, not with the technology. Data flow through the platform follows a consistent pattern that a business analyst must understand.
lessons.ch35s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment channels, hubs, engines and gateways. Payment channels are the points where customers and businesses start a payment. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch35s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement and reconciliation. Settlement is the process by which the money behind a payment actually moves between financial institutions. When a reconciliation break happens, the operations team follows a structured investigation process.
lessons.ch35s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payments certifications compared. The Payment Domain Certification is the most directly relevant certification for a business analyst working in payments, and it is offered by training providers such as . The Payment Domain Certification is the most directly relevant certification for a business analyst working in payments, and it is offered by training providers such as .
lessons.ch35s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain salary premium for payments bas. Payments business analysts in India typically earn 25 to 50 percent more than generalist business analysts with the same years of experience, and the premium grows with seniority. Payments business analysts in India typically earn 25 to 50 percent more than generalist business analysts with the same years of experience, and the premium grows with seniority.
lessons.ch35s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interview q and a for payments roles. When an interviewer asks what it means when a payment is settled, they want to hear that settlement is the final and irrevocable transfer of funds between banks to cover a payment. The final set of questions covers the business analyst side of payments.
lessons.ch35s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain your learning path forward. The eight-session learning path on this site is designed to take a business analyst from zero payments knowledge to job-ready domain expertise, and the best way to use it is in order, with practice between sessions. The eight-session learning path on this site is designed to take a business analyst from zero payments knowledge to job-ready domain expertise, and the best way to use it is in order, with practice between sessions.
lessons.ch36s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment hub architecture inside a bank. A payment hub is the central processing engine that receives payment instructions from every channel in a bank and routes each one to the correct destination. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch36s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message routing: from channel to rail. Routing begins with the information in the payment instruction itself. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch36s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain queueing and retry logic. Message queues exist because the systems in a bank do not all run at the same speed and are not all available at the same time. Apache Kafka is the newer technology, and it is used where a bank needs to stream very large volumes of events, such as logging every status change of every payment for analytics.
lessons.ch36s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reconciliation engines. A reconciliation engine compares two or more sets of records and reports the differences. The analyst starts with the payment reference and traces it through every system, the hub log, the payment engine log, the SWIFT message archive, and the core banking entries.
lessons.ch36s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exception queues. A payment lands in an exception queue when an automated check cannot be resolved by the system alone. Manual repair screens are the tools analysts use to fix these payments.
lessons.ch36s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain systems connect. APIs, or application programming interfaces, are the modern way for systems to talk to each other in real time. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch36s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain database design for payments. The payment instruction table is the core record. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch37s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain jpmorgan chase and citibank. JPMorgan Chase runs one of the largest payment operations on the planet, moving more than 10 trillion dollars a day across its wholesale payment systems. A business analyst working at either bank spends much of the time mapping fields between the old and new formats and testing that no data is lost in translation.
lessons.ch37s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hsbc and standard chartered. HSBC runs one of the largest trade and payments networks in the world, with a presence in more than 60 countries and a particular strength in Asia. A business analyst joining either bank will quickly learn that sanctions compliance is not a separate function; it is built into every step of the payment flow.
lessons.ch37s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bank of america and wells fargo. Bank of America runs its payments through a central hub that connects to every US clearing system, Fedwire for high value same-day payments, the Clearing House for ACH bulk payments, and the RTP network for real-time. For a business analyst, the lesson from both banks is that domestic scale and global reach need different architectures.
lessons.ch37s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain deutsche bank and bnp paribas. Deutsche Bank runs its payment operations from Frankfurt, with a payment hub that connects directly to TARGET2, the real-time gross settlement system of the Eurosystem, and to STEP2, the pan-European clearing system for. The lesson for a business analyst is that consolidation is a long project, often taking five years or more, and it succeeds only when the business, operations, and technology teams agree on a single target design before the migration starts.
lessons.ch37s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain barclays and natwest. Barclays runs one of the largest payment hubs in the United Kingdom, processing more than 1 billion payments a year for retail customers, corporate clients, and correspondent banks. For a business analyst, BACS is a good example of a system where the business rules matter more than the technology, the direct debit guarantee, the indemnity claim process, and the rules for failed collections are all defined by the scheme, not by the bank.
lessons.ch37s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ubs and goldman sachs. UBS payment operations are built around its private banking and wealth management business. The lesson for a business analyst is that the right technology choice depends on the client base, a wealth manager needs security and service, an investment bank needs speed and integration, and a retail bank needs volume and cost.
lessons.ch37s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain more banks and what to learn from them. Morgan Stanley is similar to Goldman Sachs in that its payment operations are built around institutional clients, but it has a different emphasis, wealth management through its acquisition of E*TRADE and its large. The patterns a business analyst should recognise are the same in every large bank.
lessons.ch38s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain banks need a canonical payment model. A large bank receives payment instructions from many different places, and each place speaks its own dialect. When each channel connects directly to each payment system, the bank must build and maintain a separate translation for every pair, and a small change in one system can break several others without warning.
lessons.ch38s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain canonical model: core entities and fields. At the centre of the canonical model sits the payment instruction, the single record that represents one instruction to move money. This central record is the anchor that every other entity connects to, and it is the record that operations teams search for when a customer asks where a payment is.
lessons.ch38s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain source-to-target mapping and field transformation. Mapping starts with a mapping table that lists each source field, the canonical field it feeds, and the rule that governs the transfer. A good mapping table is a controlled document, reviewed by business analysts, developers, and operations staff, and changed only through a formal change request so that no one edits a live mapping by accident.
lessons.ch38s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain data enrichment, normalisation and reference data. Enrichment adds information the customer did not supply, using data the bank already holds. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch38s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment identifiers, parties, accounts and amount precision. Every payment carries several identifiers, and each one has a different job. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch38s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain data lineage, retention and auditability. Data lineage records the full journey of every field in a payment, from its source to its final destination. It records the customer who created the instruction, the operator who released it, the second approver who authorised a payment above GBP 50,000, the sanctions officer who cleared a false alert, and the system that rejected a payment for an invalid IBAN.
lessons.ch38s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hands-on exercise: pain.001 to canonical model to pacs.008. Emma Wilson logs in to Barclays online banking on the morning of 5 November 2026 and creates a new international payment. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.
lessons.ch39s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain catalogue at a glance: PAIN, PACS, CAMT, admi and head. The ISO 20022 catalogue is organised into families, and each family is named by its first four letters. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.
lessons.ch39s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain customer-to-bank: pain.001, pain.002, pain.008. The pain.001 message, Customer Credit Transfer Initiation, carries a customer instruction to move money from the debtor account to one or more creditor accounts. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.
lessons.ch39s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bank-to-bank: pacs.002, pacs.003, pacs.004, pacs.008, pacs.009. The pacs.008 message, FI to FI Customer Credit Transfer, is the most widely used message in cross border payments, and it carries a customer payment from the debtor bank to the creditor bank. Returns must be processed promptly, because a return that sits unmatched can look like a missing payment, and a customer who is not told about a return may believe the supplier has been paid when the money is on its way back.
lessons.ch39s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cash management: camt.029, camt.052, camt.053, camt.054, camt.056. The camt.053 message, Bank to Customer Statement, is the formal end of day statement for an account, and it is the document a treasurer reconciles against the company ledger. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.
lessons.ch39s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message identification, correlation, group header vs transaction info. Four identifiers do most of the work in ISO 20022, and confusing them is a common source of errors. An operations analyst who can follow those identifiers across five messages can answer a customer query in minutes, while an analyst who searches only by amount may find several payments of EUR 8,750.00 and choose the wrong one.
lessons.ch39s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mandatory, optional and conditional fields, schema validation, external code sets, version management and market practice rules. Every field in an ISO 20022 message has a usage rule, mandatory, optional, or conditional. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.
lessons.ch39s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain practical exercise: transform an MT103 into pacs.008. Here is a pre-migration MT103 we will transform, sent before coexistence ended on 22 November 2025. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.
lessons.ch39s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.060: the account reporting request. A treasury team needs to know the balance of its euro account at 11 in the morning, before it decides whether to fund a large payment. For a business analyst, the camt.060 is a small message with a clear use case, and the requirements around it are straightforward.
lessons.ch39s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.057 in depth: the notification to receive. A bank that expects a large credit needs to know it is coming, so that it can plan its liquidity, match the credit when it arrives, and chase it if it does not. The message carries the facts the receiving bank needs to prepare.
lessons.ch39s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pacs.009 adv: the advice that accompanies a financial institution transfer. A pacs.009 is a financial institution credit transfer, the ISO 20022 message that moves money between banks. The ADV code sits alongside the other pacs.009 codes, and the analyst must know the set.
lessons.ch39s11: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain remt.001: the remittance advice. A payment tells the receiver that money is moving. For a business analyst, remittance advice design is reconciliation design.
lessons.ch39s12: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.035, camt.058 and camt.059: proprietary investigations and the notification to receive lifecycle. Three camt messages complete two pictures: the lifecycle of a notification to receive, and the handling of investigations that do not fit a standard format. For a business analyst, the lesson is about lifecycle and edge cases.
lessons.ch39s13: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pacs.010: the financial institution direct debit. The pacs family has a credit message for customers, the pacs.008, and a credit message for financial institutions, the pacs.009. For a business analyst, the pacs.010 requirements cover the agreement data, the authorisation check, the debit posting, and the failure handling.
lessons.ch40s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reconciliation. A payment can pass every upfront check and still end up in the wrong place, which is why reconciliation exists as an independent control after processing. For a business analyst, reconciliation is also where business knowledge meets operational reality, because every break tells a story about a process gap.
lessons.ch40s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro reconciliation. A nostro account is an account that a bank holds with another bank in a foreign currency, and its name comes from the Latin word for ours, because the money in it belongs to the holding bank. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.
lessons.ch40s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain internal ledger, clearing and settlement reconciliation. Every payment creates at least two ledger entries inside the bank, a debit and a credit, and the discipline of double-entry bookkeeping requires those entries to balance exactly. The practical lesson for analysts is that internal reconciliation is not one check but a chain of checks, and a break in any link can hide a break further down the chain.
lessons.ch40s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction-level matching: references, amounts, currencies and value dates. The payment reference is the primary key that links an internal record to an external statement line, and it must survive the whole payment journey unchanged. For example, a reference of sixteen characters sent through a system that allows only fifteen will lose its final digit, and the statement line will sit unmatched until an analyst manually links it by amount and date.
lessons.ch40s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain breaks: suspense accounts, unmatched transactions, duplicates and date mismatches. A suspense account holds funds temporarily when the bank knows money has moved but does not yet know where it belongs, and it must never become a permanent home. The operations team posts it to a suspense account, opens an investigation, and contacts the correspondent bank to ask who sent the money and why.
lessons.ch40s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain automated vs manual reconciliation and end-of-day processing. Automated reconciliation uses rules to match internal records against external statements at high speed and at high volume, and it is the only practical way to reconcile a large bank. Automation therefore removes the routine work and leaves the exceptions, which is exactly where skilled analysts add the most value.
lessons.ch40s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example and exercise: a bank sends 10,000 payments, 9,850 settled, 100 rejected, 30 returned, 20 have no corresponding settlement record. The starting point is the control total, because the engine must first prove that it is looking at the complete population before it matches anything. A return arrives as a pacs.004 message, often with reason code AC04 for a closed account or MD07 for an end customer who is deceased, and the engine matches it to the original payment by reference.
lessons.ch40s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain three-way reconciliation. Reconciliation proves that two records of the same activity agree. For a business analyst, reconciliation design is a requirements exercise with three inputs.
lessons.ch41s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exception landscape: what can go wrong. A payment exception is any payment that does not complete its intended journey cleanly, from the customer instruction to the beneficiary credit, and the scale of the problem is larger than most people expect. The exceptions range from a simple typing error in an account number to a clearing system outage that stops thousands of payments at once, and the operations team must triage them by value, by age, and by customer impact before it starts fixing them.
lessons.ch41s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain technical rejection vs business rejection. A technical rejection happens when a payment message fails a structural or format check, so the receiving system cannot even begin to process the business content. The reporting of the two types is different, and analysts must know which message to expect for each.
lessons.ch41s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment repair, return, recall and cancellation. Repair means correcting a payment that has been stopped before settlement, so that it can proceed without the customer having to start again. A payment of USD 60,000 may be held because the beneficiary address is incomplete, or because the intermediary bank details are missing, and the operations team can repair it by adding the missing information from the customer instruction or from a standing arrangement.
lessons.ch41s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigations, duplicate payments, timeouts and pending payments. An investigation begins when a customer reports that a payment has not arrived, or when reconciliation shows a payment with no matching settlement, and the analyst must reconstruct the payment journey from the available. An investigation begins when a customer reports that a payment has not arrived, or when reconciliation shows a payment with no matching settlement, and the analyst must reconstruct the payment journey from the available evidence.
lessons.ch41s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain unknown payment status, failed beneficiary credit and clearing system outage. Unknown payment status means the bank has sent a payment but has received no acknowledgement, no rejection, no return, and no settlement confirmation, so it cannot state with confidence whether the money moved. The bank must not assume the payment failed, and it must not assume it succeeded, because either assumption can cause a duplicate or a missing payment.
lessons.ch41s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 messages and reason codes for exceptions (pacs.002, pacs.004, camt.056, camt.029, pain.002 with real reason codes). The pacs.002 message, known as the payment status report, is the standard way for a bank to tell the sender whether a payment was accepted, rejected, or is still pending. Common codes include AC01 for an incorrect account number, AC04 for a closed account, AM04 for insufficient funds, AM05 for a duplicate payment, and MD07 for an end customer who is deceased.
lessons.ch41s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: trace one payment through every possible failure scenario (one USD cross-border payment traced through reject, return, recall, duplicate, timeout and outage, with what happens at each step). The payment begins as a customer instruction for USD 85,000, sent by the Mumbai company through its corporate banking channel, with the beneficiary account at a bank in New York and the value date set for 6 November. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.
lessons.ch41s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain automating exceptions and investigations. Exceptions are the work that straight through processing cannot finish: the payment that failed validation, the funds that cannot be applied, the claim that money never arrived, the return that needs a decision. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.
lessons.ch41s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message repair. Repair is the work of fixing a message that failed, so that it can proceed. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.
lessons.ch42s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment testing. Payment testing is different because every test case touches value, and value cannot be undone with a simple refresh. When a payment system sends a pacs.008 for 125,000 pounds to the wrong beneficiary account, the bank must start a recall, contact the receiving bank, and explain the error to the customer.
lessons.ch42s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain test levels: unit, SIT, UAT and regression. Unit testing checks the smallest piece of code in isolation, and in payments that precision matters. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.
lessons.ch42s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain writing test scenarios for happy path and negative path. A happy path scenario proves that the normal journey works from start to finish. If an operations user resubmits the same pain.001 file twice, or if a system retries a pacs.008 after a timeout, the bank must not send the money twice.
lessons.ch42s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain scheme certification: what schemes and clearing systems demand. Scheme certification proves that a bank can exchange payment messages correctly with a scheme or clearing system. Before a bank can join SWIFT, it must prove that its MT103 and pacs.008 messages pass validation, that it can handle acknowledgements, and that its operations team can manage exceptions.
lessons.ch42s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain test data, environments and simulators. Good test data looks like real payment data, but it must never be real customer data. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.
lessons.ch42s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain defect management, entry and exit criteria. A defect in payments must be recorded with enough detail for a developer to reproduce it without guessing. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.
lessons.ch42s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: build a UAT pack for a pacs.008 change. Start the exercise with a clear change description, because a UAT pack without a scope is impossible to sign. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.
lessons.ch42s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain boundary, time-out and duplicate testing for real-time flows. Testing a real time payment flow is different from testing a batch flow, because the flow has hard edges: amount limits that reject a payment one unit over the line, time limits that turn a slow payment into a failed. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.
lessons.ch43s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain threat model for payment systems. A threat model for payments starts with the simple fact that payment systems move money, and money attracts determined attackers. A payment operations analyst who can create, approve and release payments on their own could send 250,000 dollars to a personal account and hide the transaction.
lessons.ch43s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authentication: passwords, mfa, certificates and OAuth2. Passwords are the weakest form of authentication, yet they remain common in payment portals. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.
lessons.ch43s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain encryption in transit and at REST, key management and hsms. Encryption in transit protects payment data while it moves between systems. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.
lessons.ch43s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mTLS, API security and secure connectivity. Mutual TLS, known as mTLS, is TLS where both sides prove their identity with certificates. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.
lessons.ch43s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT customer security programme and network security. The SWIFT Customer Security Programme, known as CSP, was created after a series of high profile frauds in which attackers used stolen SWIFT credentials to send fraudulent payment instructions. The bank must log every SWIFT session, every message sent and received, and every change to configuration or user access.
lessons.ch43s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud controls, monitoring and incident response. Fraud controls start before a payment is sent, with checks that look for risk in the instruction itself. A monitoring system might flag a customer who receives a large credit and then sends the full amount onward within an hour, a pattern known as money mule activity.
lessons.ch43s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: security review of a payment API. Start the review with the integration itself, so that you know exactly what you are checking. The treasury system will send payment instructions as JSON, the bank will return a pacs.008 reference and a pacs.002 status, and the customer will check balances through a separate read only API.
lessons.ch43s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system authentication: OAuth2 grants, scopes, token lifetimes and certificate rotation. System authentication is how one system proves its identity to another, and it is different from customer authentication in kind, not just in degree. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the scope for each operation, the scope each client type is entitled to, and the error returned when a client asks for a scope it does not have.
lessons.ch44s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain day in payment operations. A payment operations day starts before most customers wake up, because the first files and instructions are already waiting in the queues. When it does not, an analyst opens the repair screen, reads the error code, fixes the missing beneficiary account number and releases the payment again.
lessons.ch44s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cut-off management and processing calendars. A cut-off time is the last moment a payment instruction can be accepted for processing on a given value date. A customer who submits a payment of 500,000 pounds at 5 past 5 in the afternoon for CHAPS will therefore see a value date of the next working day, even though the money leaves the account immediately.
lessons.ch44s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain end-of-day processing, close and start-of-day checks. End of day processing begins when the last clearing system closes and no new same day payments can be released.
