lessons.ch92s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ACH in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. ACH is the workhorse of US payments, and the SEC code is the first thing an analyst checks.
lessons.ch92s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain same Day ACH and apply it to a real banking scenario. Same Day ACH changed US business payments, and the windows are the operational fact that matters.
lessons.ch92s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FedNow in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. FedNow is the newest US rail, and the analyst must know when it fits and when it does not.
lessons.ch92s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain RTP from The Clearing House and apply it to a real banking scenario. Two instant systems means routing decisions, and the analyst writes the routing logic.
lessons.ch92s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain the US faster payments landscape and apply it to a real banking scenario. Routing across US rails is the treasurer daily decision, and the analyst must map it.
lessons.ch92s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FEDWIRE and CHIPS message detail: the fields that carry a US payment. United States high value payments run on two systems, Fedwire and CHIPS, and each carries field level detail that decides routing, validation, and tracking. For a business analyst, field level mapping between Fedwire, CHIPS, and ISO 20022 is core work.
lessons.ch92s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain zelle: bank-owned instant person-to-person payments. Zelle is the United States bank owned person to person payment network. For a business analyst, Zelle teaches the alias pattern, the instant and irrevocable trade off, and the scam problem.
lessons.ch92s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain epn: the electronic payments network. The United States Automated Clearing House, the ACH network, has two operators. For a business analyst, EPN and the ACH network teach the batch pattern and the operator model.
lessons.ch93s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SCT in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. SCT is the default SEPA credit transfer, and its timeline is the baseline every analyst knows.
lessons.ch93s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SCT Inst in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. SCT Inst is now a mainstream rail, and the 10-second rule is a hard obligation.
lessons.ch93s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SDD in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. SDD is the recurring payment scheme of Europe, and the refund rules are its core.
lessons.ch93s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain TIPS in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. TIPS is the settlement engine for European instant payments, and its liquidity model is the key fact.
lessons.ch93s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain verification of Payee and apply it to a real banking scenario. Verification of Payee is the fraud control that the regulation made mandatory, and the analyst must know its outcomes.
lessons.ch93s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain the European Payments Council rulebooks and apply it to a real banking scenario. The EPC change cycle is the calendar that drives SEPA implementation work.
lessons.ch93s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA scheme participation, reachability, the EPC register and what happens when a bank is not reachable and apply it to a real banking scenario. Reachability is the directory of SEPA, and the analyst uses it to check whether a payment can arrive.
lessons.ch93s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA one leg out: when one leg leaves SEPA. The SEPA schemes assume both legs of a payment are inside the Single Euro Payments Area: the payer bank and the payee bank are both SEPA participants, and the payment travels under SEPA rules from end to end. For a business analyst, a One Leg Out corridor is a mapping exercise with a boundary.
lessons.ch94s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain correspondent banking in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. Correspondent banking is the plumbing of cross-border payments, and its decline is reshaping the market.
lessons.ch94s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT gpi in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. gpi changed customer expectations, and the tracker is now a standard service.
lessons.ch94s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CBPR+ and the MT to MX migration and apply it to a real banking scenario. CBPR+ is the biggest messaging change in decades, and the analyst must know the translation rules.
lessons.ch94s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain serial versus cover payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. Serial versus cover is the core routing decision in cross-border payments, and the analyst must know both.
lessons.ch94s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain foreign exchange in cross-border payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. FX is where cross-border payments make or lose money, and the analyst must price it correctly.
lessons.ch94s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro account optimisation and apply it to a real banking scenario. Nostro optimisation is a direct profit lever, and the analyst quantifies the saving.
lessons.ch94s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross-border instant payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. Cross-border instant is the future of the market, and the links are the new infrastructure.
lessons.ch94s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sanctions and compliance in cross-border payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. De-risking is the unintended consequence of tougher compliance, and the analyst must measure it.
lessons.ch94s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain eurogiro and tipanet: postal and cooperative bank networks. The payment landscape is not only SWIFT and correspondent banking. For a business analyst, niche networks are a reminder that the payment landscape has many layers.
lessons.ch94s10: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sadc-rtgs and comesa: regional settlement in southern and eastern africa. Most cross border payments in Africa settle in dollars or euros, through correspondent banks outside the continent, even when the trade is between two African countries. For a business analyst, regional settlement systems are a study in integration patterns.
lessons.ch95s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain AML screening in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. Name screening is the first line of defence, and its false positive rate decides whether the operations team can cope.
lessons.ch95s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sanctions screening in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. The 50 percent rule is the most commonly failed sanctions test, and it needs ownership data the bank must collect.
lessons.ch95s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain when a sanctions hit fires and apply it to a real banking scenario. The sanctions hit workflow is the most time-critical operational process in payments, and it must be rehearsed.
lessons.ch95s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud detection in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. Fraud detection is a behaviour problem, and the analyst writes the rules that describe normal behaviour.
lessons.ch95s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud case handling step by step and apply it to a real banking scenario. Fraud case handling is a race against time, and the workflow must be drilled, not improvised.
lessons.ch95s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain APP scams and mule accounts and apply it to a real banking scenario. Mule networks are the infrastructure of fraud, and dismantling them stops many scams at once.
lessons.ch95s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction monitoring in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. Monitoring tuning is a continuous discipline, and the analyst owns the evidence for every change.
lessons.ch95s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain controls operations in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. Controls are only real if they are tested, and the test result is the evidence the auditor asks for.
lessons.ch95s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fatca, gatca and the common reporting standard. FATCA, GATCA and the Common Reporting Standard are three names that describe two regimes and one nickname, and keeping them apart is the starting point for the whole topic. A US person includes a US citizen wherever they live, a US tax resident, and certain US entities, and the bank must also look through foreign entities to substantial US owners.
lessons.ch96s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai, machine learning and generative ai actually are. Let us start by clearing up three words that get thrown around as if they mean the same thing, because they do not. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch96s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain machine learning works, at the level a BA needs. Machine learning sounds technical, but the idea is simple, and you already understand it from your own work. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch96s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain generative ai and large language models. Generative AI is the technology behind the chat tools you have probably already tried. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch96s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai agents: what they do and how they differ from a chatbot. A chatbot answers questions. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch96s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai can do well in payments. AI earns its place in payments when the work is high volume, repetitive, and pattern-based, and when a wrong answer is cheap to catch. A payments operations team handles 40,000 customer queries a month.
lessons.ch96s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai cannot do. AI has hard limits, and a BA who does not know them will sign off on a design that fails in production. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch96s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain vocabulary of ai: a ba's glossary. You cannot challenge a vendor or write a requirement if you do not share the words, so here is the vocabulary you will actually hear in payments AI projects, each in one plain sentence. The guardrail says any score above 80 goes to a human in the loop, so an analyst reviews it instead of the system deciding alone.
lessons.ch96s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hype versus reality. Every new technology arrives with hype, and AI has arrived with more hype than most, so a BA needs a way to separate a real capability from a sales pitch. The AI will replace your analysts.
lessons.ch96s9: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain multi-agent systems and crewai. A single AI agent can do a great deal, but some tasks are better done by several agents working together, each with a role, collaborating toward a result no single agent achieves as well. Agents have roles, goals, and backstories: a senior payments analyst, a compliance reviewer, a technical writer.
lessons.ch97s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain using ai to draft a BRD. A business requirements document is the hardest artefact to start, and that is exactly where AI helps most, as long as you treat its output as a first draft and never as a finished document. Walk the flow end to end, ask the operations team what breaks, and add the rules and exceptions the draft missed.
lessons.ch97s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain using ai to write user stories and acceptance criteria. User stories are a good job for AI, because the format is simple and the tool has seen thousands of examples, but the acceptance criteria are where the value lives, and that is where you must check hardest. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch97s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain using ai for process maps and flow diagrams. AI can draft a process map quickly, but a process map is only useful if every leg and every branch is present, and AI is very good at producing a map that looks complete while quietly dropping a branch. So use AI to draw the first version, then walk it with the operations team, step by step, and add every missing leg and branch before anyone builds from it.
lessons.ch97s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain using ai to generate test cases and UAT scenarios. Test cases are one of the best uses of AI in BA work, because the tool is good at volume and at combinations a person would take hours to list, but only if you tell it what coverage means for your flow. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch97s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reviewing and validating ai output: the quality gate. Every AI output that goes into a project needs a quality gate, and the gate is a person, not another AI tool. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch97s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain failure modes: hallucinated fields and missing legs. This is a real case from the industry, and it is the most important lesson in this chapter. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch97s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain prompt patterns that work for payments BA work. A good prompt is not a clever trick. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch97s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain to never let ai decide alone. There is a clear line in payments BA work, and it is this. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch98s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain owning an ai product in payments. Owning an AI product is not the same as owning a regular feature, and the difference matters from the first day. If the model changes after retraining, or the data feeding it changes, the same payment might be treated differently next week, and your customer will notice.
lessons.ch98s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain defining the problem and the ai use case. Every AI feature should start from a business problem, not from the technology. Take a payments operations team that spends three hours every morning sorting payment exceptions.
lessons.ch98s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain data requirements for an ai feature. An AI feature is only as good as the data behind it, so the product owner has to treat data as a requirement, not as something the engineers will sort out later. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch98s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain model requirements and evaluation. Before you accept an AI model, you have to agree what good looks like, in numbers, and how you will test it. If it wrongly flags a genuine payment of 850 pounds, the customer is annoyed and the operations team does extra work, but no money is lost.
lessons.ch98s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain acceptance criteria for ai features. Acceptance criteria for an AI feature have to be testable, and they have to cover failure as well as success. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch98s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain guardrails and human-in-the-loop design. Guardrails are the rules that decide where the model may act alone, where a human must approve, and how the handoff between the two works. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch98s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain managing the ai product backlog. Managing an AI product backlog is different from managing a normal backlog, because the work splits into four kinds that compete for the same team, and if you treat them as one list, the visible work always wins. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch98s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain measuring an ai feature: the metrics that matter. You cannot own an AI feature without measuring it, and you cannot measure it with one number. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch99s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain control framework for ai that touches money. When AI touches money, it needs the same control discipline as any system that moves money, and that discipline rests on four separations that must stay apart. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch99s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain approval limits and authorisation. Approval limits and authorisation are the two controls that stop a single mistake, or a single bad decision, from becoming a large loss. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch99s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain control ownership: naming the owner. Every AI control needs a named human owner. If no one owns that control, the operations team works around it, the holds pile up, and customers start calling.
lessons.ch99s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain audit trails and explainability. An audit trail is the record that lets you explain, after the fact, why an AI system did what it did with money. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch99s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain regulatory expectations for ai in payments. Regulators expect the same control discipline for AI as for any system that moves money. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch99s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain EUR 12,000 invoice case: authorisation. This is a real case from the industry, and it shows what happens when the control that makes a payment safe is given to the very thing it is meant to control. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch99s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain EUR 8,000 API calls case: spend caps. This is a real case from the industry, and it shows how a thousand tiny payments can add up to a large loss when no one sets a limit. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch99s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain EUR 60,000 pilot case: control ownership. This is a real case from the industry, and it shows why an award is not a control. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch100s1: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in reconciliation matching. Reconciliation is proving that the money that left the bank matches the money that was supposed to leave, and AI helps by matching payments to statements faster than a person can by hand. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch100s2: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in exception prediction. An exception is a payment that did not go through cleanly, and AI in exception prediction tries to spot the payments likely to fail before they fail, so the operations team can act early instead of fixing the mess. An exception is a payment that did not go through cleanly, and AI in exception prediction tries to spot the payments likely to fail before they fail, so the operations team can act early instead of fixing the mess afterwards.
lessons.ch100s3: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in fraud detection. Fraud detection is the job of spotting a payment that looks wrong before the money is gone, and AI helps by scoring each payment against patterns it has learned from past fraud and from normal behaviour. Take a retail customer who normally spends around three thousand rupees a day in Bangalore, and suddenly there is a payment of one lakh eighty thousand rupees to a new beneficiary in another country at two in the morning.
lessons.ch100s4: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in customer service for payments. Customers ask the same payment questions again and again, where is my money, why has it not arrived, what is the charge, and AI can answer many of those questions fast, but only inside clear limits. Imagine a customer who sent fifteen thousand rupees by an instant payment at ten in the morning and asks at noon where it is.
lessons.ch100s5: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain writing requirements for ai systems. Writing requirements for an AI feature is different from writing requirements for a normal screen or report, because you describe not only what the system must do, but how it must behave when it is uncertain, and what. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.
lessons.ch100s6: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain defining success metrics and handling ai failures. An AI feature is not done when it goes live, it is done when you can prove it works, and that proof needs numbers, a review rhythm, and a plan for when it gets things wrong. That is the rollback, and it must be a button the operations team can press, not a change request that takes three weeks.
lessons.ch100s7: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone brief: design an ai-assisted payments feature. This is your capstone brief, the task that pulls the whole AI course together into one piece of work you can show. A good example is AI assisted reconciliation of cross border payments, where a corporate client sends one payment of twelve thousand dollars to cover thirty invoices in different currencies, and the operations team spends hours matching the statement lines, the charges and the exchange rate differences by hand.
lessons.ch100s8: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone: specify it end to end. In this final lesson you turn your capstone idea into a full specification, the document a developer, a tester and an operations manager can actually work from. First, the BRD outline, one page that states the business problem, the users, the current process, the proposed AI feature, the benefits in numbers, and the risks, for example cutting the unmatched queue from forty items a week to ten, and saving six hours of analyst time a week.

courses.integrated: The flagship. Everything in the academy, all 10 parts. The complete Payments Training Hub academy in one course: all 10 parts, 99 chapters and 874 narrated lessons, from what a payment is to payment hub architecture, ISO 20022 and SWIFT messaging, clearing and settlement, cards, compliance, APIs, exceptions, reconciliation and the BA and PO professional practice. You will be able to: Explain what a payment is and trace it from instruction to beneficiary credit; Read and write ISO 20022 and SWIFT messages field by field; Design payment APIs and integration requirements; Investigate exceptions, returns and recalls; Run reconciliation and operational controls; Compare settlement models and recommend one for a bank; Design a payment hub architecture; Do the BA job end to end and deliver the capstone.
courses.part-1: What a payment is, and how the ecosystem fits together. Start here. You will be able to: Explain what a payment is and how it differs from a transfer and from settlement; Name the payment instruments and when each is used; Describe the payment ecosystem and the parties in it; Trace a payment through its lifecycle end to end; Explain what money is, how accounts hold balances, and how cheques and paper instruments still work.
courses.part-10: CBDCs, stablecoins, AI, and where payments goes next. The future part. You will be able to: Explain CBDCs, stablecoins and tokenised deposits; Explain AI in reconciliation, fraud, customer service and operations; Explain embedded finance and use ISO 20022 data for analytics; Assess what is real and what is hype in payments innovation.
courses.part-2: India, US, Europe and UK rails, plus TARGET and TIPS. How money actually moves in each market. You will be able to: Explain how UPI, IMPS, NEFT and RTGS work in India; Explain Fedwire, FedNow, ACH and CHIPS in the US; Explain SEPA, T2, T2S and TIPS in Europe; Explain Faster Payments, CHAPS and BACS in the UK; Compare real-time payment systems across markets and recommend a rail for a corridor.
courses.part-3: MT and MX messages, field by field, with real examples. The messaging part. You will be able to: Read SWIFT MT messages field by field; Read and write ISO 20022 messages (pacs.008, pain.001, pain.002, camt.052, camt.053, camt.054, camt.060); Map MT messages to ISO 20022 and explain CBPR+ migration; Validate an ISO 20022 XML file against its schema; Handle rejects and returns with pacs.002 and pacs.004.
courses.part-4: How international payments really work, end to end. The cross-border part. You will be able to: Explain correspondent banking and nostro/vostro accounts; Compare serial and cover payments and choose between them; Calculate what a beneficiary receives under OUR, SHA and BEN; Explain FX rates, spreads and conversion, and track a payment with SWIFT gpi and UETR; Handle cross-border exceptions, rejects, returns and investigations.
courses.part-5: Clearing is not settlement. Learn the difference properly. The settlement part. You will be able to: Explain clearing and netting, and compare RTGS, deferred net settlement and prefunded models; Explain liquidity management, intraday credit and settlement risk; Reconcile a payment against its statement and find the break; Explain ledger posting, cash management, and how clearing systems work, including when settlement fails; Calculate a net settlement position.
courses.part-6: Sanctions, AML, exceptions, returns and the daily ops grind. The controls part. You will be able to: Explain sanctions screening, name matching, AML, KYC and fraud prevention; Investigate a payment exception to its resolution and handle returns, recalls and claims; Explain payment security, GDPR, BSA/AML rules and operational resilience; Run screening, fraud and sanctions operations, and apply the AI governance control framework; Communicate an incident to the people who need to know.
courses.part-7: Authorisation, clearing, settlement, wallets and POS. The cards part. You will be able to: Explain card authorisation, clearing and settlement; Explain 3D Secure, tokenisation and chargebacks; Compare Visa and Mastercard network rules; Explain digital wallets, POS systems, recurring payments and 3RI.
courses.part-8: Hubs, platforms, gateways and integration, the engineering view. The architecture part. You will be able to: Design a payment hub architecture, including state, resilience and control; Design a payment API contract in OpenAPI, including idempotency and error handling; Explain event-driven payment architecture, integration patterns, and payment engine internals and observability; Design for resilience and disaster recovery, and explain OAuth2 and mTLS for payment APIs; Plan payment testing and scheme certification.
courses.part-9: Requirements, stories, BRDs, workshops, AI, and the capstone. The BA part. You will be able to: Gather requirements and write BRDs, FSDs and Jira user stories for payments changes; Map messages, run workshops, and write test cases for a payments project; Use AI to draft BA artifacts, and validate what it produces; Own an AI product: define the use case, the data and model requirements, the guardrails and the metrics; Deliver the capstone: a full business analysis deliverable for a payments change.
